Geometry-Aware Diffusion Approximate Posterior Sampling for Sparse-View and Limited-Angle CT

Honglei Brinkmann    Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb    Ander Biguri Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK.
Abstract

Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and acquisition time and may mitigate motion artifacts. However, angular undersampling provides insufficient information to determine the image uniquely and stably. Limited-angle CT, arising from restricted angular coverage, produces strongly directional information loss associated with the missing angular range. In both settings, image directions may be strongly observed, weakly constrained, or unobservable, leading to severe ill-posedness and reconstruction ambiguity. Existing diffusion-based approaches incorporate measurement information through likelihood guidance, data-consistency operations, or range–null-space corrections. However, they do not generally use the continuously varying measurement sensitivity of the acquisition to jointly shape both reconstruction updates and stochastic exploration.

We propose a geometry-aware diffusion-guided stochastic reconstruction framework for sparse-view and limited-angle CT. Its central component is a regularized noise-weighted pullback metric constructed from the CT forward operator and measurement-noise covariance. This metric continuously adapts both the measurement-aware update and stochastic exploration according to directional measurement sensitivity, suppressing changes along strongly constrained directions while permitting greater exploration along weakly constrained and unobservable directions. We complement this geometry-aware update with a regularized data-consistency correction and approximately null-space-restricted stochastic perturbations, implemented matrix-free using forward and backprojection operations together with conjugate-gradient solves. Experiments on sparse-view, noisy, and limited-angle CT demonstrate competitive reconstruction quality, strong measurement consistency, and spatially resolved empirical uncertainty estimates.

1 Introduction

Reducing radiation dose and acquisition time remains a central objective in CT and motivates sparse-view imaging, in which projections are acquired at only a small number of angles. Limited-angle CT arises from a different acquisition constraint: projections are unavailable over a contiguous angular range because of physical or geometric restrictions. Although the two settings produce different patterns of information loss, both leave many image directions unobservable or weakly constrained. Depending on the acquisition geometry and discretization, the corresponding forward operator may be rank deficient or severely ill-conditioned, resulting in an exact null space or a collection of directions that have only a small effect on the measurements.

From an inverse-problem perspective, this loss of information creates intrinsic ambiguity. Different images may produce identical noiseless measurements or measurement differences too small to distinguish from noise. The measured sinogram therefore cannot uniquely and stably determine the unknown image, and prior information or regularization is required to obtain a plausible reconstruction [52, 3].

Classical CT reconstruction methods include analytical methods such as filtered back projection (FBP) [26] and iterative methods such as ART [16], SART [2], and statistical model-based iterative reconstruction [13, 49]. Under incomplete acquisition, iterative methods commonly combine a data-fidelity term with regularization based on assumptions such as image smoothness, sparsity, or piecewise constancy. Representative examples include total-variation and other sparsity-promoting formulations [41, 12]. Although these methods improve stability, their performance depends on the selected regularizer, and overly restrictive regularization may remove fine anatomical structures, particularly under severe angular undersampling [63, 50]. Moreover, these methods usually produce a single reconstruction and do not quantify the uncertainty in image components that are weakly constrained or unobservable from the measurements [25, 47].

Between classical regularization and fully learned reconstruction, plug-and-play priors [54] and regularization by denoising [37] incorporate an external denoiser into an iterative reconstruction algorithm. These frameworks are not inherently learning-based, because the denoiser may be either handcrafted or learned.

More recently, learning-based methods have introduced data-driven image models into CT reconstruction. Representative approaches include supervised reconstruction networks [24], unrolled reconstruction networks [1], deep image priors [53, 33], and implicit neural representations [42, 44]. The latter two approaches optimize a network for the observed data and therefore do not necessarily require paired training images.

These methods can achieve strong reconstruction quality [40]. However, supervised methods require representative training data and may be sensitive to changes in anatomy, acquisition geometry, or noise level. Methods such as deep image priors and implicit neural representations do not require training on an external dataset. Instead, they represent the unknown image with a neural network whose parameters are fitted directly to each input sinogram through the CT forward model. Moreover, many of these approaches return a single reconstruction and do not directly characterize ambiguity caused by missing or noisy measurements.

Diffusion and score-based models learn distributions of clean images and can therefore provide learned prior information for inverse problems. At each diffusion timestep, a pretrained diffusion model estimates the score of the noisy-image distribution obtained from clean CT images. This score provides a time-dependent learned prior direction that guides reconstruction toward plausible clean images. Measurement information can then be incorporated through conditional reverse transitions, likelihood-gradient guidance, or explicit data-consistency operations [46, 27, 7]. For example, DDRM constructs operator-conditioned reverse transitions for linear inverse problems [27]; DPS incorporates the measurement likelihood through gradient guidance [7]; DDS incorporates conjugate-gradient data-consistency updates into diffusion sampling [8]; and ReSample applies an optimization-based hard data-consistency step followed by stochastic resampling [43].

Diffusion models have also been applied to incomplete-view CT through sinogram restoration, image-domain degradation models, likelihood-guided sampling, and iterative data-consistency corrections [60, 6, 32, 17]. A related family of methods exploits range–null-space structure, separating image components that affect the measured sinogram from components that are invisible to the acquisition. DDNM [57] uses a pseudoinverse to impose data consistency on the measurement-sensitive range-space component of each diffusion estimate while retaining null-space content predicted by the diffusion model. RN-SDE [18] and its noise-aware extension RNSD+ [19] use a trained diffusion process to recover information missing from limited-angle measurements and repeatedly correct the component that is visible in the acquired data. The conditional score-based null-space (CSN) model [62] similarly uses a score model to estimate missing image information while using an iterative least-squares step to enforce agreement with the measured projections. Like DDNM, these methods use range–null-space-based corrections that treat the data-visible and measurement-invisible components separately: measurement information corrects the range-space component, whereas the learned diffusion model estimates or retains the complementary null-space component.

In contrast, our method does not make a binary range–null-space separation its primary sampling mechanism. It uses a regularized noise-weighted pullback metric to continuously adapt both guided updates and stochastic exploration across image directions according to their measurement sensitivity. Approximate null-space exploration and regularized data-consistency correction are complementary components of this geometry-aware framework.

Although these methods improve incomplete-view CT reconstruction, they do not fully account for the fact that incomplete measurements constrain some image directions strongly, other directions only weakly, and exact null-space directions not at all. Existing methods use the forward operator through likelihood guidance, data-consistency optimization, or separate range–null-space corrections. However, they do not generally use the same continuously varying measurement sensitivity to govern both the measurement-aware update and stochastic exploration.

In this work, we develop a geometry-aware diffusion-guided stochastic reconstruction framework for sparse-view and limited-angle CT. Its central component is a regularized noise-weighted pullback metric constructed from the CT forward operator and measurement-noise covariance. The metric continuously adapts the measurement-aware update and stochastic exploration according to the sensitivity of each image direction to the acquired data: directions that strongly affect the measured sinogram receive smaller updates and less stochastic variation, whereas weakly constrained directions receive relatively greater exploration. The framework additionally includes approximate null-space exploration and regularized data-consistency correction, both evaluated matrix-free through forward and backprojection operations together with conjugate-gradient solves.

Contributions.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

  • •

    We propose a geometry-aware diffusion-guided stochastic reconstruction framework for sparse-view and limited-angle CT, combining a learned image prior with a noise-weighted measurement likelihood. Its central component is a regularized noise-weighted pullback metric that continuously adapts both the measurement-aware update and stochastic exploration according to directional measurement sensitivity.

  • •

    We complement the whole-space metric update with approximate null-space exploration and a regularized data-consistency correction. All required inverse actions are evaluated matrix-free using forward and backprojection operations together with conjugate-gradient solves, without explicitly forming a Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.

  • •

    We demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive reconstruction quality, strong agreement with the measured data, and spatially resolved empirical uncertainty estimates under sparse-view, noisy, and limited-angle CT acquisition.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews diffusion-based inverse-problem methods and incomplete-view CT approaches, positioning the proposed framework within the existing literature. Section 3 first formulates the incomplete-view CT posterior and its directional measurement geometry, and then develops the proposed pullback-metric sampling framework, its data-consistency correction, and approximate null-space exploration. Section 4 evaluates reconstruction quality, measurement consistency, empirical sample variability, and the individual roles of the geometry-aware components. Section 5 concludes the paper. The appendices A provide supporting derivations, implementation details, and supplementary experimental results.

2 Related Work

Diffusion priors for inverse problems.

Diffusion and score-based generative models provide learned image priors for ill-posed inverse problems. The score-based SDE framework formulates generation as a reverse-time stochastic process and provides a general basis for incorporating measurement information during sampling [46]. DDRM constructs operator-conditioned reverse transitions for linear inverse problems [27], whereas DPS uses approximate likelihood-gradient guidance for noisy linear and nonlinear inverse problems [7]. MCG and Π\PiGDM refine conditional-score guidance through manifold-constrained and pseudoinverse-inspired constructions, respectively [9, 45]. Other approaches combine pretrained diffusion models with optimization or consistency operations, including DDS, ReSample, PSLD, and DMPlug [8, 43, 38, 56].

Riemannian MCMC methods.

Riemannian Langevin methods form a class of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods in which a metric determines how far the sampler moves and how much random perturbation it adds in different parameter-space directions [15]. Thus, they provide a general principle for using geometry to shape both deterministic and stochastic sampling components. Our framework uses this principle in a different setting: diffusion-guided reconstruction from incomplete CT measurements. Rather than constructing a general state-dependent posterior metric, we derive a noise-weighted pullback geometry from the CT forward operator and measurement-noise covariance. This geometry represents the directional sensitivity of the particular CT acquisition and is used to adapt the measurement-aware update and stochastic exploration during reconstruction.

Diffusion models for incomplete-view CT.

Several diffusion models have been developed specifically for sparse-view and limited-angle CT. CT-SDM models view reduction through a deterministic sinogram-domain degradation process, whereas CvG-Diff learns to reverse image-domain artifacts caused by angular undersampling [60, 6]. Other methods use sinogram-domain generation, spatial-frequency representations, projection conditioning, or physics-informed score models [32, 17, 35, 20]. These approaches show that diffusion priors can effectively reduce incomplete-view artifacts. They typically encode the acquisition geometry through a learned degradation, restoration, or conditioning process. In contrast, our framework incorporates the CT forward operator and measurement-noise model directly into the reconstruction dynamics. The resulting noise-weighted pullback geometry continuously adapts both the measurement-aware update and stochastic exploration according to directional measurement sensitivity.

Data consistency and range–null-space methods.

Explicit data-consistency operations are widely used in diffusion-guided reconstruction. DDS combines diffusion sampling with conjugate-gradient data-consistency updates, while ReSample alternates diffusion generation, optimization-based consistency correction, and resampling [8, 43]. These operations can reduce disagreement with the acquired data. However, by themselves, they do not provide a common continuously varying noise-weighted geometry for both the measurement-aware reconstruction update and stochastic exploration across strongly and weakly observed image directions.

A related family of methods uses range–null-space structure. For each diffusion estimate, DDNM uses the acquired measurements and a pseudoinverse to correct the image content that affects the measurements. It retains the remaining measurement-invisible content from the diffusion model [57]. RN-SDE uses a conditional mean-reverting diffusion process to reconstruct limited-angle CT images and repeatedly applies a range–null-space correction: the data-visible content is adjusted using the acquired measurements, while the missing content is inferred by the learned model [18]. Its extension RNSD+ addresses noisy limited-angle CT by treating missing views as a sinogram-inpainting problem and introducing a noise-aware rectification mechanism [19]. Similarly, CSN combines conditional score-based reconstruction with iterative least-squares data consistency so that missing information is estimated principally in the null space [62]. These methods conceptually treat data-visible and measurement-invisible components separately.

In contrast, our framework does not first decompose each diffusion estimate into range-space and null-space components in order to construct its primary sampling update. Instead, the main diffusion-guided update is defined over the whole image space and is continuously adapted by a regularized noise-weighted pullback metric. We then use complementary range–null-space-inspired operations: a regularized data-consistency correction modifies the measurement-sensitive component, whereas an approximately null-space-restricted perturbation promotes additional exploration in weakly constrained and unobservable directions. Thus, range–null-space structure is used in supporting data-consistency and null-space-exploration steps rather than as a binary decomposition underlying the main update.

3 Method

In sparse-view and limited-angle CT, the measurements constrain some image directions more, while other directions are less constrained or unobservable. We therefore propose a diffusion-score-guided stochastic reconstruction framework that uses the CT forward operator and noise covariance to adapt both the direction and scale of each sampling update according to noise-weighted measurement sensitivity. The framework reduces the measurement residual through a regularized data-consistency correction. At the same time it concentrates stochastic exploration along weakly constrained and unobservable directions, where reconstruction ambiguity remains.

The proposed method is presented in six parts. We first introduce the forward model, the noise-weighted posterior, and the resulting anisotropy between strongly observed, weakly constrained, and unobservable image directions in Section 3.1. Section 3.2 uses this geometry to construct pullback-metric-preconditioned Langevin dynamics in place of standard isotropic sampling. Section 3.3 describes the orthogonal decomposition of the image space into range-space (containing directions that affect the measurements) and null-space (containing directions that are invisible to the forward operator). Section 3.4 introduces a regularized Riemannian data-consistency correction that avoids requiring an explicitly available generalized inverse. Section 3.5 introduces approximately null-space-restricted stochastic perturbations that promote exploration along weakly constrained and unobservable image directions while suppressing changes in the measured sinogram.

Finally, Section 3.6 combines all components into an iterative sampling procedure that (i) preconditions diffusion updates using the measurement-induced pullback metric, (ii) reduces the measurement residual through a regularized data-consistency correction, and (iii) controls stochastic exploration according to the measurement sensitivity of different image directions, thus supporting spatial uncertainty estimation.

3.1 Problem Formulation and Posterior Geometry

In the context of CT reconstruction, our goal is to recover images from projection measurements acquired through a forward operator. The CT measurements constrain different image directions to different degrees: some directions strongly affect the measured sinogram, whereas others are weakly constrained or completely unobservable. We formulate sparse-view and limited-angle CT reconstruction as Bayesian inference. A posterior formulation combines the information provided by the measurements with a learned image prior and allows the remaining ambiguity to be represented by multiple reconstruction samples.

We consider sparse-view and limited-angle CT reconstruction under the linear forward model:

y=AΩ​x+ε,y\;=\;A_{\Omega}x+\varepsilon, (1)

where x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the unknown image, AΩ∈ℝm×nA_{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is the forward operator restricted to a subset of view angles Ω\Omega, y∈ℝmy\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is the measured log-sinogram. The measurement error is modeled as

ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),

where Σ∈ℝm×m\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is the measurement-noise covariance matrix and Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0.

Remark.

Origin of the Gaussian noise model. Under the idealized Beer–Lambert model, the expected photon count at detector bin ii is [48, 58]

λi=I0​e−(AΩ​x)i,\lambda_{i}\;=\;I_{0}\,e^{-(A_{\Omega}x)_{i}}, (2)

where I0I_{0} is the incident photon count. The detected count is modeled as

Yi∼Poisson⁡(λi).Y_{i}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{i}).

For sufficiently large transmitted counts, applying the logarithmic transform to the photon measurements gives the approximate post-log Gaussian model

y≈AΩ​x+ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),Σ=diag​(1λi)i=1m.y\;\approx\;A_{\Omega}x+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),\qquad\Sigma\;=\;\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\lambda_{i}}\right)_{i=1}^{m}. (3)

Thus, highly attenuated rays have lower transmitted photon counts and larger log-domain noise variance. The ideal count-based plug-in precision is λ^i=I0​e−yi\widehat{\lambda}_{i}=I_{0}e^{-y_{i}}. In practice, we use the stabilized, normalized, and clipped effective precision described in Appendix A.1.

Sparse-view CT acquires projections at fewer angular views while typically retaining the full angular coverage, whereas limited-angle CT restricts the angular range over which projections are acquired. Let AΩ∈ℝm×nA_{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, where nn is the dimension of the image space and mm is the dimension of the measurement space. Depending on the acquisition geometry and discretization, AΩA_{\Omega} may be rank deficient or severely ill-conditioned.

The null-space of the forward operator is

𝒩⁡(AΩ)={v∈ℝn:AΩ​v=0}.\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega})\;=\;\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:A_{\Omega}v=0\right\}. (4)

By the rank–nullity theorem,

dim𝒩⁡(AΩ)=n−rank⁡(AΩ).\dim\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega})\;=\;n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{\Omega}). (5)

When m<nm<n, we have rank⁡(AΩ)≤m<n\operatorname{rank}(A_{\Omega})\leq m<n, so a nontrivial null-space is guaranteed. For any v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}),

AΩ​(x+v)=AΩ​x.A_{\Omega}(x+v)\;=\;A_{\Omega}x. (6)

Thus, an image change along vv is completely invisible to the forward operator.

In the presence of measurement noise, however, directions outside the exact null space may produce sinogram changes that are difficult to distinguish from noise. Under the Gaussian measurement model, the likelihood is

p(y∣x)∝exp(−12‖Σ−1/2(AΩx−y)‖22).p(y\mid x)\propto\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right). (7)

The covariance Σ\Sigma accounts for the different noise levels of the sinogram measurements.

Let p0​(x)p_{0}(x) denote the learned distribution of clean CT images. Bayes’ rule gives

p(x∣y)∝p0(x)exp(−12‖Σ−1/2(AΩx−y)‖22).p(x\mid y)\propto p_{0}(x)\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right). (8)

The posterior combines the learned image prior with noise-weighted measurement information [47]. Posterior sampling therefore uses the prior to explore image components that are unobservable or only weakly constrained by the measurements.

To quantify the measurement sensitivity along a unit-norm direction v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, ‖v‖2=1\|v\|_{2}=1, consider the perturbed image x+a​vx+av, where a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R} controls the perturbation magnitude. The second derivative of the negative log-likelihood Φ(x):=12‖Σ−1/2(AΩx−y)‖22\Phi(x):=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right\|_{2}^{2} with respect to aa is

d2d​a2Φ(x+av)=v⊤AΩ⊤Σ−1AΩv=‖Σ−1/2AΩv‖22.\frac{d^{2}}{da^{2}}\Phi(x+av)\;=\;v^{\top}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}v\;=\;\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}A_{\Omega}v\right\|_{2}^{2}. (9)

This quantity is the likelihood curvature along vv and measures how strongly the direction affects the measurements relative to the noise.

We refer to these directions as effective null-space directions. Therefore, the exact null-space describes completely unobservable directions, whereas the effective null-space additionally captures directions that are only weakly observable relative to the noise.

Because the quantity in Equation (9) depends on the perturbation direction vv, we can see that the likelihood induces an anisotropic geometry: strongly observed, weakly constrained, and unobservable directions receive different amounts of measurement information. The total posterior uncertainty is determined jointly by this measurement information and the learned prior, since the prior may still constrain directions that are invisible to the forward operator. Under a Laplace approximation around a posterior mode x⋆x^{\star}, the posterior is locally approximated by a Gaussian whose precision is the Hessian of the negative log-posterior:

Hpost​(x⋆)=Hprior​(x⋆)+AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ,H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})\;=\;H_{\mathrm{prior}}(x^{\star})+A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}, (10)

where Hprior​(x⋆)=−∇x2​log⁡p0​(x⋆)H_{\mathrm{prior}}(x^{\star})\;=\;-\nabla_{x}^{2}\log p_{0}(x^{\star}) is the local curvature contributed by the prior. For any v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}),

v⊤​Hpost​(x⋆)​v=v⊤​Hprior​(x⋆)​v,v^{\top}H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})v\;=\;v^{\top}H_{\mathrm{prior}}(x^{\star})v, (11)

because the measurement contribution vanishes along vv. For a weakly constrained direction, the measurement contribution in Equation (9) is nonzero but small. A formal statement and proof are provided in Appendix A.3, Proposition 3. This measurement-induced geometry motivates the geometry-aware sampling framework developed in the following subsection, which adapts the sampling dynamics to the noise-weighted sensitivity of different image directions.

3.2 Geometry-Aware Diffusion Sampling via a Pullback Metric

As discussed in Section 3.1, the likelihood constrains different image directions to different degrees. It provides strong information along well-observed directions, limited information along weakly constrained directions, and no direct information along exact null-space directions. Standard isotropic Langevin dynamics [29], which combine gradient-based drift with Gaussian noise for posterior sampling [36], do not account for these differences because their stochastic term has the same variance in every image direction. We therefore construct a Riemannian metric from the CT forward operator and effective noise precision to adapt both the deterministic and stochastic updates to measurement sensitivity.

To construct the metric, consider a small image perturbation δ​x∈ℝn\delta x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Under the linear forward model, it produces the measurement perturbation

δ​y=AΩ​δ​x.\delta y\;=\;A_{\Omega}\delta x.

The Gaussian likelihood in (7) is

p⁡(y∣x)∝exp⁡(−12​(AΩ​x−y)⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y)).p(y\mid x)\;\propto\;\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right).

Here, Σ\Sigma denotes the measurement-noise covariance used during reconstruction, estimated as described in Appendix A.1. Its inverse Σ−1≻0\Sigma^{-1}\succ 0 is called the precision matrix. Because Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} is symmetric positive definite, it defines an inner product on the measurement space 𝒴=(ℝm,⟨⋅,⋅⟩𝒴)\mathcal{Y}=(\mathbb{R}^{m},\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}})

⟨u,v⟩𝒴:=u⊤​Σ−1​v,u,v∈ℝm.\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}\;:=\;u^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}v,\qquad u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. (12)

Under the conditionally independent noise model used in this work, Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} is diagonal, so the inner product can be written as

⟨u,v⟩𝒴=∑i=1m(Σ−1)i​i​ui​vi.\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\Sigma^{-1})_{ii}u_{i}v_{i}. (13)

Each diagonal entry (Σ−1)i​i(\Sigma^{-1})_{ii} represents the effective precision of measurement bin ii. Measurements with higher precision receive greater weight, whereas noisier measurements with lower precision receive less weight. Thus, ∥⋅∥𝒴\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{Y}} measures a sinogram perturbation relative to the reliability of the measurements.

Pullback metric on image space.

The inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩𝒴\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}} defines a geometry on the measurement space ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, but the unknown image xx lives in the image space ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. To transfer this geometry to the image space, we use the concept of a pullback metric [30, 11], a standard construction in differential geometry that transports a metric from one space to another via a smooth map. Given a small image perturbation δ​x∈ℝn\delta x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the forward operator AΩA_{\Omega} maps it to the corresponding measurement perturbation δ​y=AΩ​δ​x∈ℝm\delta y=A_{\Omega}\,\delta x\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. The significance of δ​x\delta x in image space can then be assessed by measuring the significance of its image δ​y\delta y in measurement space under ⟨⋅,⋅⟩𝒴\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}. Pulling the measurement-space inner product back through AΩA_{\Omega} gives

⟨δ​x1,δ​x2⟩G:=⟨AΩ​δ​x1,AΩ​δ​x2⟩𝒴=δ​x1⊤​G​δ​x2,G=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ.\langle\delta x_{1},\delta x_{2}\rangle_{G}\;:=\;\langle A_{\Omega}\delta x_{1},A_{\Omega}\delta x_{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{Y}}\;=\;\delta x_{1}^{\top}G\delta x_{2},\qquad G=A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}. (14)

This bilinear form measures image perturbations according to how strongly and reliably they affect the measured sinogram. The matrix GG is symmetric positive semi-definite (a pullback pseudo-metric on the image space), not a genuine Riemannian metric. It is singular whenever 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}) is nontrivial, because

G​v= 0for every ​v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ).Gv\;=\;0\qquad\text{for every }v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}).

We therefore define the regularized metric

Gγ=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​I,γ>0,G_{\gamma}\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}\;+\;\gamma I,\qquad\gamma>0, (15)

The regularization shifts every eigenvalue of GG by γ\gamma, making GγG_{\gamma} symmetric positive definite. Directions with data-dependent eigenvalues much larger than γ\gamma are only slightly affected and retain their measurement-dependent weighting. Along exact null-space directions, the measurement-induced term vanishes because the measurements contribute no information. Only the isotropic Euclidean regularization γ​I\gamma I remains. By contrast, weakly constrained directions retain a small measurement-dependent contribution together with this regularization.

Having defined the measurement-induced metric GγG_{\gamma}, we now incorporate it into posterior sampling. Langevin dynamics provide a natural framework because they combine gradient-based guidance toward a target density with stochastic exploration. We first consider an ideal continuous-time process with access to the exact posterior score and then derive the practical diffusion-guided approximation used in our algorithm.

Pullback-Preconditioned Langevin Dynamics.

Let Xτ∈ℝnX_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the random image state at continuous sampling time τ\tau, and let π⁡(x)=p⁡(x∣y)\pi(x)=p(x\mid y) be the target posterior density. Standard isotropic overdamped Langevin dynamics combine deterministic drift along the gradient of the log-target density with isotropic Brownian noise [36]:

d​Xτ=∇log⁡π​(Xτ)​d​τ+2​d​Wτ,dX_{\tau}\;=\;\nabla\log\pi(X_{\tau})\,d\tau+\sqrt{2}\,dW_{\tau}, (16)

where WτW_{\tau} is an nn-dimensional standard Brownian motion. The first term is the deterministic drift, while the second is the stochastic term. Over a small time interval Δ​τ\Delta\tau, the stochastic term contributes a Gaussian increment with covariance 2​Δ​τ​In2\Delta\tau I_{n}, where In∈ℝn×nI_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the identity matrix on the image space. It therefore applies the same variance in every image direction.

The process is constructed to have π\pi as an invariant density: if X0X_{0} has density π\pi, then XτX_{\tau} has the same density for every τ≥0\tau\geq 0, as verified below.

To incorporate the measurement geometry, we precondition both the drift and the stochastic term using Gγ−1G_{\gamma}^{-1}:

dXτ=Gγ−1∇logπ(Xτ)dτ+2​Gγ−1dWτ.dX_{\tau}\;=\;G_{\gamma}^{-1}\nabla\log\pi(X_{\tau})\,d\tau+\sqrt{2G_{\gamma}^{-1}}\,dW_{\tau}. (17)

The first term is the geometry-preconditioned drift, while the second is the geometry-shaped stochastic term. These dynamics suppress variation along directions with high noise-weighted measurement sensitivity and permit larger updates along weakly constrained and unobservable directions.

To ensure that the geometry-aware preconditioning changes the sampling dynamics without changing the target posterior, we verify that π\pi remains an invariant density of the ideal continuous process.

Let ρτ​(x)\rho_{\tau}(x) denote the probability density of XτX_{\tau}. For a stochastic differential equation of the form

d​Xτ=b⁡(Xτ)​d​τ+B​d​Wτ,dX_{\tau}\;=\;b(X_{\tau})\,d\tau+B\,dW_{\tau},

where b:ℝn→ℝnb:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is the drift function and B∈ℝn×nB\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a constant diffusion matrix, the corresponding Fokker–Planck equation is [34]

∂τρτ=−∇⋅(bρτ)+12∇⋅(BB⊤∇ρτ).\partial_{\tau}\rho_{\tau}\;=\;-\nabla\!\cdot\left(b\,\rho_{\tau}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\nabla\!\cdot\left(BB^{\top}\nabla\rho_{\tau}\right).

For Equation (17),

b(x)=Gγ−1∇logπ(x),BB⊤= 2Gγ−1.b(x)\;=\;G_{\gamma}^{-1}\nabla\log\pi(x),\qquad BB^{\top}\;=\;2G_{\gamma}^{-1}.

Substituting these expressions gives

∂τρτ\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\rho_{\tau} =−∇⋅(Gγ−1ρτ∇logπ)+∇⋅(Gγ−1∇ρτ).\displaystyle\;=\;-\nabla\!\cdot\left(G_{\gamma}^{-1}\rho_{\tau}\nabla\log\pi\right)+\nabla\!\cdot\left(G_{\gamma}^{-1}\nabla\rho_{\tau}\right).

To test stationarity, set ρτ=π\rho_{\tau}=\pi. Since

∇logπ=∇ππ,andπ∇logπ=∇π,\nabla\log\pi\;=\;\frac{\nabla\pi}{\pi},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\pi\nabla\log\pi\;=\;\nabla\pi,

we obtain

∂τρτ|ρτ=π=−∇⋅(Gγ−1∇π)+∇⋅(Gγ−1∇π)= 0.\displaystyle\left.\partial_{\tau}\rho_{\tau}\right|_{\rho_{\tau}=\pi}\;=\;-\nabla\!\cdot\left(G_{\gamma}^{-1}\nabla\pi\right)+\nabla\!\cdot\left(G_{\gamma}^{-1}\nabla\pi\right)\;=\;0.

Therefore, if X0X_{0} has density π\pi, then XτX_{\tau} has density π\pi for every τ≥0\tau\geq 0. Hence, π\pi is an invariant density of the ideal continuous dynamics. A formal statement and the corresponding conditions are provided in Appendix A.5.

Diffusion-score approximation.

The ideal dynamics in Equation (17) require the exact posterior score. From the posterior factorization, this score has the form

∇log⁡π​(x)=∇log⁡p0​(x)−∇Φ​(x),\nabla\log\pi(x)\;=\;\nabla\log p_{0}(x)-\nabla\Phi(x),

where the data-fidelity gradient ∇Φ​(x)\nabla\Phi(x) can be evaluated from the known forward operator, measured sinogram, and fixed noise precision, whereas the clean-image prior score ∇log⁡p0​(x)\nabla\log p_{0}(x) is not available analytically. We use a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) [23] pretrained on clean CT images. During pretraining, Gaussian noise is added to the images at different diffusion timesteps, and the model learns to predict the added noise. During reconstruction, the model parameters remain fixed, and the predicted noise is used to estimate the image-prior score that guides the reconstruction toward plausible CT images.

Let x(k)x^{(k)} denote the current reconstruction at sampling iteration kk, and let tkt_{k} be the corresponding DDPM timestep. For simplicity, all image variables below are expressed in the normalized intensity range used during diffusion-model training.

At each iteration, we treat x(k)x^{(k)} as the current estimate of the clean image and apply the standard DDPM forward-noising equation:

xtk(k)=α¯tk​x(k)+1−α¯tk​ϵ(k),ϵ(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,In),x_{t_{k}}^{(k)}\;=\;\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t_{k}}}\,x^{(k)}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{k}}}\,\epsilon^{(k)},\qquad\epsilon^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}), (18)

where α¯tk\bar{\alpha}_{t_{k}} is the cumulative product of the DDPM noise schedule up to timestep tkt_{k}. The variable xtk(k)x_{t_{k}}^{(k)} is the noisy image supplied to the pretrained diffusion model.

For an ϵ\epsilon-prediction DDPM, the network ϵθ​(xtk(k),tk)\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t_{k}}^{(k)},t_{k}) predicts the Gaussian noise contained in xtk(k)x_{t_{k}}^{(k)}. The corresponding score estimate is [23, 46]

s(k)=−ϵθ​(xtk(k),tk)1−α¯tk,s^{(k)}\;=\;-\frac{\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t_{k}}^{(k)},t_{k})}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t_{k}}}}, (19)

which approximates ∇xtk​log​ptk​(xtk(k))\nabla_{x_{t_{k}}}\log p_{t_{k}}(x_{t_{k}}^{(k)}). This score supplies the learned image-prior direction at noise level tkt_{k}.

The data-fidelity gradient is evaluated at the current reconstruction x(k)x^{(k)}:

g(k):=∇Φ​(x(k))=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x(k)−y),g^{(k)}\;:=\;\nabla\Phi(x^{(k)})\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\left(A_{\Omega}x^{(k)}-y\right), (20)

where

Φ⁡(x)=12​(AΩ​x−y)⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y).\Phi(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y). (21)

We combine the DDPM score and data-fidelity gradient as

r(k)=λk​s(k)−μk​g(k),r^{(k)}\;=\;\lambda_{k}s^{(k)}-\mu_{k}g^{(k)}, (22)

where λk\lambda_{k} and μk\mu_{k} control the relative strengths of the learned prior and measurement guidance. The DDPM score is evaluated at the noisy image xtk(k)x_{t_{k}}^{(k)}, whereas the data-fidelity gradient is evaluated at the current reconstruction x(k)x^{(k)}. Therefore, r(k)r^{(k)} is used as a practical combined guidance direction rather than an exact diffusion-time posterior score.

Geometry-preconditioned update.

The pullback-metric-preconditioned direction u(k)u^{(k)} is obtained by solving

Gγ​u(k)=r(k),Gγ=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​In.G_{\gamma}u^{(k)}\;=\;r^{(k)},\qquad G_{\gamma}\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n}. (23)

The current reconstruction is then updated according to

x~(k)=x(k)+αk​u(k),x~(k)←x~(k)+νG(k),νG(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,2​αk​Gγ−1),\tilde{x}^{(k)}\;=\;x^{(k)}+\alpha_{k}u^{(k)},\qquad\tilde{x}^{(k)}\leftarrow\tilde{x}^{(k)}+\nu_{G}^{(k)},\qquad\nu_{G}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,2\alpha_{k}G_{\gamma}^{-1}\right), (24)

where αk>0\alpha_{k}>0 is the sampling step size. The deterministic term αk​u(k)\alpha_{k}u^{(k)} combines the learned DDPM prior with the noise-weighted data-fidelity gradient, while νG(k)\nu_{G}^{(k)} provides metric-shaped stochastic exploration.

Because the evolving reconstruction x(k)x^{(k)} is not itself maintained as a DDPM noisy state, we apply the forward-noising equation before each score evaluation. This produces an input whose noise level is consistent with the assigned DDPM timestep tkt_{k}. The resulting score provides annealed prior guidance, ranging from coarse structure at high noise levels to finer details at low noise levels. This procedure differs from a standard DDPM reverse trajectory, since a newly noised state is constructed from the current reconstruction at each iteration.

Matrix-free implementation via conjugate gradient.

The preconditioned direction in (23) is computed by solving a linear system of the general form

Gγ​u=r,G_{\gamma}u\;=\;r, (25)

where r∈ℝnr\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is known and u=Gγ−1​r∈ℝnu=G_{\gamma}^{-1}r\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the unknown. We solve this via the conjugate gradient (CG) method [22, 21] (Appendix A.4.1), which avoids forming Gγ∈ℝn×nG_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} explicitly. CG requires only matrix-vector products with GγG_{\gamma}. Expanding the definition Gγ=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​IG_{\gamma}=A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I and applying it to a search direction pp gives

Gγ​p\displaystyle G_{\gamma}p =(AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​I)​p\displaystyle\;=\;\bigl(A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I\bigr)p
=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ​p+γ​p\displaystyle\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}p+\gamma p
=AΩ⊤​(Σ−1​(AΩ​p))+γ​p.\displaystyle\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}p)\bigr)+\gamma p. (26)

Each CG iteration requires one forward projection and one backprojection, together with diagonal precision weighting. Since Gγ≻0G_{\gamma}\succ 0, the linear system has a unique solution and is suitable for conjugate gradient. In exact arithmetic, CG recovers this solution in at most nn iterations. In practice, it is terminated when the residual falls below a prescribed tolerance. The regularization parameter γ\gamma bounds the smallest eigenvalue away from zero and improves numerical conditioning.

To sample νG(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,2​αk​Gγ−1)\nu_{G}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2\alpha_{k}G_{\gamma}^{-1}) matrix-free, draw independent standard Gaussian vectors ξ(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,Im)\xi^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}) in measurement space and c(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,In)c^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) in image space, and form

w(k)=AΩ⊤Σ−1/2ξ(k)+γc(k)∼𝒩(0,Gγ).w^{(k)}\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1/2}\xi^{(k)}+\sqrt{\gamma}\,c^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\gamma}). (27)

Solving Gγ​z(k)=w(k)G_{\gamma}z^{(k)}=w^{(k)} and setting νG(k)=2​αk​z(k)\nu_{G}^{(k)}=\sqrt{2\alpha_{k}}\,z^{(k)} gives νG(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,2​αk​Gγ−1)\nu_{G}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2\alpha_{k}G_{\gamma}^{-1}). This covariance is exact when the linear system is solved exactly. With a finite CG tolerance, the generated covariance approximates 2​αk​Gγ−12\alpha_{k}G_{\gamma}^{-1}, with accuracy determined by the linear-solve residual. The full correctness proof is given in Appendix A.5, Lemma 2.

The update (24) is anisotropic because the measurement-induced metric preconditions both the deterministic direction and the stochastic covariance. It suppresses stochastic variation and prior-driven updates along strongly observed directions while allowing greater variation along weakly constrained and unobservable directions. The resulting variability is determined jointly by the measurement geometry and the learned prior. The regularized data-consistency correction and additional approximately null-space-restricted perturbations are introduced in Sections 3.4 and 3.5, respectively.

3.3 Orthogonal Direct Sum Decomposition

To exploit the geometric structure of AΩA_{\Omega} explicitly, we need a precise definition of how image space splits into measurement-constrained and measurement-invisible directions. The orthogonal direct sum decomposition[39, 4, 5] provides this definition, and the two subspaces identified by it will correspond directly to the two components of the sampling process in Sections 3.4 and 3.5.

The forward operator maps the image space to the measurement space:

AΩ:ℝn→ℝm.A_{\Omega}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}. (28)

Accordingly, ℛ⁡(AΩ)⊆ℝm\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} lies in the measurement space and describes sinograms that can be produced by the forward model. To describe measurement-sensitive directions in the image space, we instead use ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)⊆ℝn\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Proposition 1 (Orthogonal decomposition).

For any AΩ∈ℝm×nA_{\Omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the image space admits the orthogonal direct-sum decomposition

ℝn=ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)⊕𝒩⁡(AΩ).\mathbb{R}^{n}\;=\;\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})\oplus\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}). (29)

Equivalently,

ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)=𝒩​(AΩ)⟂.\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})\;=\;\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega})^{\perp}. (30)

Here, ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) contains image directions that can affect the measurements, whereas 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}) contains directions that are invisible to the forward operator. A proof is provided in Appendix A.2.

Consequently, every image x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} has a unique decomposition

x=xR+xN,xR∈ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤),xN∈𝒩⁡(AΩ).x\;=\;x_{R}+x_{N},\qquad x_{R}\in\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}),\qquad x_{N}\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}). (31)

Because AΩ​xN=0A_{\Omega}x_{N}=0, the predicted sinogram depends only on the range-space component:

AΩ​x=AΩ​xR.A_{\Omega}x\;=\;A_{\Omega}x_{R}. (32)

If the equation AΩ​x=yA_{\Omega}x=y is feasible, then every exactly measurement-consistent image can be written as

x=xdc+v,xdc∈ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤),v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ),x\;=\;x_{\mathrm{dc}}+v,\qquad x_{\mathrm{dc}}\in\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}),\qquad v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}), (33)

where xdcx_{\mathrm{dc}} is the unique range-space component satisfying AΩ​xdc=yA_{\Omega}x_{\mathrm{dc}}=y. The measurements therefore determine the range-space component under the exact feasible constraint, while the null-space component remains unidentifiable from the measurements alone.

Under the noisy likelihood used in this work, the distinction is not strictly binary. The likelihood provides no information along exact null-space directions, but it may provide only weak information along directions associated with small noise-weighted singular values. Moreover, the learned prior can influence both range-space and null-space components. The decomposition in (31) therefore describes exact algebraic observability, while the pullback metric also accounts for continuously varying measurement sensitivity.

This structure motivates the two subsequent components of the method. The regularized data-consistency correction in Section 3.4 acts along ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}), while the stochastic perturbation in Section 3.5 concentrates variation along weakly constrained and unobservable directions.

3.4 Data Consistency via Riemannian Gradient Projection

Although the geometry-aware update incorporates the measurements through the data-fidelity gradient, one Langevin update can move it away from measurement consistency. We therefore seek a correction x+x^{+} that remains close to the intermediate estimate x~\tilde{x} while reducing its mismatch with the measured sinogram yy.

Define the data-fidelity functional and its Euclidean gradient:

Φ⁡(x)=12​(AΩ​x−y)⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y),∇Φ​(x)=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y).\Phi(x)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y),\qquad\nabla\Phi(x)\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y). (34)

Under the pullback metric Gγproj=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γproj​IG_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}=A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}I, the Riemannian gradient of Φ\Phi is

gradGγprojΦ(x)=Gγproj−1∇Φ(x)=Gγproj−1AΩ⊤Σ−1(AΩx−y).\operatorname{grad}_{G_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}\Phi(x)\;=\;{G^{-1}_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}\nabla\Phi(x)\;=\;{G^{-1}_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y). (35)

We use a separate regularization parameter γproj>0\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}>0 for the data-consistency correction. This parameter controls the trade-off between measurement agreement and numerical stability. It is distinct from the pullback-metric parameter γ\gamma used in the diffusion update and the null-space parameter γnull\gamma_{\mathrm{null}} used in Section 3.5.

For sparse-view and limited-angle CT, AΩA_{\Omega} may be rank deficient or severely ill-conditioned. We therefore formulate data consistency directly as the regularized proximity problem

x+=arg⁡minx​{12​‖x−x~‖22+τ2​‖AΩ​x−y‖Σ2},‖v‖Σ2:=v⊤​Σ−1​v,x^{+}\;=\;\arg\min_{x}\left\{\tfrac{1}{2}\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}^{2}+\tfrac{\tau}{2}\|A_{\Omega}x-y\|_{\Sigma}^{2}\right\},\qquad\|v\|_{\Sigma}^{2}:=v^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}v, (36)

where τ>0\tau>0 controls the strength of data consistency.

To obtain the minimizer, we define

J⁡(x)=12​‖x−x~‖22+τ2​(AΩ​x−y)⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y).J(x)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\|x-\tilde{x}\|_{2}^{2}+\tfrac{\tau}{2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y). (37)

Differentiating J⁡(x)J(x) with respect to xx gives

∇J​(x)=x−x~+τ​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y).\nabla J(x)\;=\;x-\tilde{x}+\tau A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y). (38)

At the minimum x=x+x=x^{+}, this gradient is zero. Therefore,

x+−x~+τ​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x+−y)= 0.x^{+}-\tilde{x}+\tau A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x^{+}-y)\;=\;0. (39)

Rearranging the terms gives

(In+τ​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ)​x+=x~+τ​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​y.\left(I_{n}+\tau A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}\right)x^{+}\;=\;\tilde{x}+\tau A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}y. (40)

Setting γproj=1/τ\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}=1/\tau and rearranging yields

x+=x~−Gγproj−1​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x~−y),Gγproj=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γproj​In.x^{+}\;=\;\tilde{x}-{G^{-1}_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}\tilde{x}-y),\qquad{G_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}=A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}I_{n}. (41)

Equation (41) is also one unit Riemannian-gradient step,

x+=x~−gradGγproj⁡Φ⁡(x~),x^{+}\;=\;\tilde{x}-\operatorname{grad}_{G_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}\Phi(\tilde{x}), (42)

so the data-consistency correction and the Langevin drift use the same pullback geometry. Since Gγproj{G_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}} is symmetric positive definite for every γproj>0\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}>0, the correction is well-defined regardless of the rank of AΩA_{\Omega}. For finite γproj\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}, it improves measurement consistency but does not generally enforce AΩ​x+=yA_{\Omega}x^{+}=y exactly.

The term Gγproj−1​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x~−y){G^{-1}_{\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}}}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}\tilde{x}-y) in the update (41) lies in ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) by construction, so the update modifies only the measurement-sensitive component of x~\tilde{x} while leaving its null-space component intact. This is complementary to the geometry-aware diffusion update, in which the projection enforces near-hard measurement fidelity, while the diffusion dynamics govern prior-driven reconstruction and uncertainty exploration in the null-space.

Remark (Regularized data consistency under noisy measurements).

For a measured sinogram yy, define the exact consistency set

𝒞y:={x∈ℝn:AΩ​x=y}.\mathcal{C}_{y}\;:=\;\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:A_{\Omega}x=y\right\}. (43)

This set is nonempty if and only if y∈ℛ⁡(AΩ)y\in\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}). When it is nonempty, 𝒞y\mathcal{C}_{y} is a closed affine subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, rather than a curved manifold. If y∉ℛ⁡(AΩ)y\notin\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}), then no image can reproduce the measured sinogram exactly.

Under the noisy measurement model y=AΩ​x⋆+εy=A_{\Omega}x^{\star}+\varepsilon, exact consistency may be infeasible because the noise realization ε\varepsilon need not lie in ℛ⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}). Even when the constraint is feasible, enforcing AΩ​x+=yA_{\Omega}x^{+}=y exactly fits the noisy measurement and may introduce noise-related features into the reconstruction.

The update in (41) is therefore implemented as a regularized data-consistency correction rather than an exact projection. It is well-defined for every γproj>0\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}>0, regardless of the rank of AΩA_{\Omega} or the feasibility of the exact constraint. Smaller values of γproj\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}} produce stronger agreement with the measurements along observable directions, whereas larger values give a weaker and more strongly regularized correction with improved numerical conditioning.

3.5 Approximately Null-Space-Restricted Stochastic Sampling

The regularized data-consistency correction in Section 3.4 acts along measurement-sensitive directions in ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) and does not directly modify the exact null-space component. Reconstruction ambiguity may therefore remain along exact null-space directions and along directions that are only weakly constrained relative to the measurement noise. To explore this ambiguity, we introduce stochastic perturbations that retain more variation along weakly constrained and unobservable directions while suppressing measurement-sensitive components.

Exact null-space invariance.

Suppose that xx satisfies AΩ​x=yA_{\Omega}x=y. For any v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}),

AΩ​(x+v)=AΩ​x+AΩ​v=y.A_{\Omega}(x+v)\;=\;A_{\Omega}x+A_{\Omega}v\;=\;y. (44)

Thus, an exact null-space perturbation does not change the predicted sinogram. An exact orthogonal projection onto 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}) can be expressed using the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the discretized forward operator. Although this pseudoinverse exists mathematically, accurately applying it can be computationally demanding for large-scale and ill-conditioned CT systems. We therefore use a regularized approximation based on forward and backprojection operations.

Approximate null-space perturbation.

At reconstruction iteration kk, we draw

ζ(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,In),\zeta^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}), (45)

where InI_{n} is the n×nn\times n identity matrix. The isotropic random vector ζ(k)\zeta^{(k)} generally contains components along both measurement-sensitive and null-space directions.

We represent its measurement-sensitive component approximately as AΩ⊤​q(k)A_{\Omega}^{\top}q^{(k)}, where q(k)∈ℝmq^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is a measurement-space coefficient vector. We therefore seek a perturbation of the form

v(k)=ζ(k)−AΩ⊤​q(k).v^{(k)}\;=\;\zeta^{(k)}-A_{\Omega}^{\top}q^{(k)}. (46)

Requiring exact null-space membership would give

AΩ​v(k)\displaystyle A_{\Omega}v^{(k)} =AΩ​ζ(k)−AΩ​AΩ⊤​q(k)\displaystyle=\;A_{\Omega}\zeta^{(k)}-A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}q^{(k)} (47)
= 0,\displaystyle=\;0,

and hence

AΩ​AΩ⊤​q(k)=AΩ​ζ(k).A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}q^{(k)}\;=\;A_{\Omega}\zeta^{(k)}. (48)

Because AΩ​AΩ⊤A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top} may be singular or severely ill-conditioned, we replace this system with the noise-weighted regularized system

(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γnull​Σ)​q(k)=AΩ​ζ(k),γnull>0.\left(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}\Sigma\right)q^{(k)}\;=\;A_{\Omega}\zeta^{(k)},\qquad\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}>0. (49)

Because Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0 and γnull>0\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}>0, the matrix in (49) is symmetric positive definite, even when AΩA_{\Omega} is rank deficient. It can therefore be solved using conjugate gradient.

Combining (46) and (49) gives

v(k)=[In−AΩ⊤​(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γnull​Σ)−1​AΩ]​ζ(k).v^{(k)}\;=\;\left[I_{n}-A_{\Omega}^{\top}\left(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}\Sigma\right)^{-1}A_{\Omega}\right]\zeta^{(k)}. (50)

The same perturbation can equivalently be written in image space as

v(k)=γnull​(AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γnull​In)−1​ζ(k).v^{(k)}\;=\;\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}\left(A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}I_{n}\right)^{-1}\zeta^{(k)}. (51)

To explain the filtering effect, let ϕi\phi_{i} be an eigenvector of AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩA_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega} with eigenvalue μi≥0\mu_{i}\geq 0. Along this direction,

γnull​(AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γnull​In)−1​ϕi=γnullμi+γnull​ϕi.\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}\left(A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}I_{n}\right)^{-1}\phi_{i}\;=\;\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}}{\mu_{i}+\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}}\phi_{i}. (52)

If μi=0\mu_{i}=0, then AΩ​ϕi=0A_{\Omega}\phi_{i}=0, so ϕi\phi_{i} is an exact null-space direction and its component is retained. If μi\mu_{i} is large, the direction is strongly constrained by the noise-weighted measurements and its random component is strongly suppressed. If μi\mu_{i} is small but nonzero, the direction is weakly constrained and its component is partially retained.

For finite γnull>0\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}>0, the perturbation is not generally an exact null-space vector. Indeed, using (49),

AΩ​v(k)\displaystyle A_{\Omega}v^{(k)} =AΩ​ζ(k)−AΩ​AΩ⊤​q(k)\displaystyle=\;A_{\Omega}\zeta^{(k)}-A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}q^{(k)} (53)
=γnull​Σ​q(k).\displaystyle=\;\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}\Sigma q^{(k)}.

Thus, v(k)v^{(k)} may change the predicted sinogram. The parameter γnull\gamma_{\mathrm{null}} controls the regularized filtering of measurement-sensitive components. As γnull→0\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}\to 0, the spectral factors approach one for exact null-space directions and zero for directions with μi>0\mu_{i}>0. Therefore, the operator in (50) approaches the orthogonal projector onto 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}).

Remark.

The eigenvalue analysis is used only to explain the filtering effect. No eigenvectors or eigenvalues are computed in practice. Instead, q(k)q^{(k)} is obtained by solving (49) using conjugate gradient. Each iteration requires applications of the forward operator, the backprojection operator, and the diagonal noise covariance. No pseudoinverse or dense matrix is formed explicitly.

Sampling update.

The approximately null-space-restricted perturbation is added to the intermediate reconstruction according to

x~(k)←x~(k)+βk​v(k),\tilde{x}^{(k)}\leftarrow\tilde{x}^{(k)}+\beta_{k}v^{(k)}, (54)

where βk≥0\beta_{k}\geq 0 controls the perturbation magnitude. Because v(k)v^{(k)} is only approximately null-space restricted, this update may change the predicted sinogram. The subsequent regularized data-consistency correction reduces the resulting measurement residual before producing x(k+1)x^{(k+1)}.

3.6 Overall Algorithm

The components introduced above are combined into the iterative reconstruction procedure summarized in Algorithm 1. Algorithm 1 begins from an initial reconstruction x(0)=Initialize⁡(y)x^{(0)}=\operatorname{Initialize}(y) (Line 1). The initialization may be obtained using FBP, an iterative reconstruction method, an approximate inverse, or another suitable procedure. The algorithm then performs TT reconstruction iterations (Lines 2–28), with one DDPM timestep tkt_{k} assigned to each iteration kk.

DDPM score and geometry-preconditioned update (Lines 3–9). At iteration kk, the algorithm first draws ϵ(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,In)\epsilon^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) (Line 3) and constructs a noisy version of the current reconstruction using the DDPM forward-noising equation (Line 4). The pretrained ϵ\epsilon-prediction network then provides the DDPM score estimate s(k)s^{(k)} at timestep tkt_{k} (Line 5).

The data-fidelity gradient g(k)g^{(k)} is evaluated at the current reconstruction x(k)x^{(k)} (Line 6). The DDPM score and data-fidelity gradient are combined to form the guidance direction r(k)r^{(k)} (Line 7). Because these two terms are evaluated at different states, r(k)r^{(k)} is a practical combined guidance direction rather than an exact diffusion-time posterior score.

The pullback-metric-preconditioned direction u(k)u^{(k)} is obtained using a conjugate-gradient solve (Line 8). The resulting direction is applied with step size αk\alpha_{k} to produce the intermediate estimate x~(k)\tilde{x}^{(k)} (Line 9).

Metric-shaped Langevin noise (Lines 10–15). When Langevin noise is enabled (Line 10), the algorithm draws independent standard Gaussian vectors in the measurement and image spaces (Line 11). These vectors are combined to form w(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,Gγ)w^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\gamma}) (Line 12). Solving Gγ​z(k)=w(k)G_{\gamma}z^{(k)}=w^{(k)} by conjugate gradient (Line 13) gives z(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,Gγ−1)z^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\gamma}^{-1}) when the system is solved exactly. The scaled perturbation 2​αk​z(k)\sqrt{2\alpha_{k}}\,z^{(k)} is then added to the intermediate estimate (Line 14). This produces stochastic variation whose covariance is adapted to the measurement-induced geometry.

Approximately null-space-restricted perturbation (Lines 16–21). When null-space perturbation is enabled (Line 16), the algorithm draws an isotropic image-space vector ζ(k)\zeta^{(k)} (Line 17). It then solves the noise-weighted regularized measurement-space system for q(k)q^{(k)} (Line 18). Subtracting the estimated measurement-sensitive component gives

v(k)=ζ(k)−AΩ⊤​q(k)v^{(k)}\;=\;\zeta^{(k)}-A_{\Omega}^{\top}q^{(k)} (55)

(Line 19). The perturbation is added with magnitude βk\beta_{k} (Line 20).

For finite γnull>0\gamma_{\mathrm{null}}>0, v(k)v^{(k)} is only approximately in 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}). It suppresses components that strongly affect the measurements while retaining more variation along weakly constrained and unobservable directions.

Regularized data-consistency correction (Lines 22–27). The correction is applied according to the projection schedule (Line 22). At a scheduled iteration, the algorithm solves the regularized measurement-space system for η(k)\eta^{(k)} (Line 23) and backprojects this vector to update the reconstruction (Line 24). The correction acts in ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) and reduces the measurement residual without directly modifying the exact null-space component.

Because γproj>0\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}}>0, this operation is a regularized near-hard data-consistency correction rather than an exact orthogonal projection. When no correction is scheduled, the intermediate estimate is passed directly to the next iteration (Lines 25–26).

After completing all TT iterations, the algorithm returns the final reconstruction x(T)x^{(T)} (Line 29).

The ideal continuous Langevin process in Section 3.2 has the target posterior as an invariant distribution under the stated assumptions. Algorithm 1 additionally uses a DDPM-based approximate guidance direction, finite step sizes, finite-tolerance CG solves, approximately null-space-restricted perturbations, and scheduled data-consistency corrections. It should therefore be interpreted as a practical geometry-aware stochastic reconstruction procedure rather than an exact discretization of the ideal posterior dynamics.

The sequences {αk}\{\alpha_{k}\}, {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\}, {μk}\{\mu_{k}\}, and {βk}\{\beta_{k}\} may be constant or scheduled over the reconstruction iterations. In our implementation, each quantity is constant by default; a user-specified schedule can vary its value between the beginning and end of sampling. The exact values and schedules used in each experiment are reported in the implementation details.

4 Experiments

We evaluate the proposed geometry-aware approximate diffusion posterior sampling framework on sparse-view and limited-angle CT reconstruction. The experiments have three goals. First, we assess reconstruction quality by comparing against the DM4CT benchmark [40] using the standard distortion metrics PSNR and SSIM, and additionally provide qualitative comparisons across a range of acquisition degradations. Second, we evaluate whether the proposed method produces informative empirical sample variability rather than only a single point estimate, analysing the uncertainty structure of our method. Third, we verify the central geometry-aware claim: that posterior variability is suppressed in measurement space and concentrated in directions that are either invisible to the acquisition geometry or corrupted by measurement noise.

Experiments are conducted on the medical CT data from the 2016 Low Dose Grand Challenge, following the data preprocessing and evaluation protocol used in DM4CT. Unless otherwise stated, stochastic reconstructions are generated from the same measured sinogram. For noisy configurations, the measurement noise realization is fixed and only the sampler seed varies between samples, ensuring that observed variability reflects posterior uncertainty rather than changes in the measurement itself.

4.1 Reconstruction Performance

We evaluate reconstruction performance from two complementary perspectives. First, we compare against existing methods on the standard DM4CT benchmark, reporting PSNR and SSIM to enable direct quantitative comparison with the published benchmark results (Section 4.1.1). Second, we provide qualitative comparisons across a controlled set of acquisition degradations, to isolate how different kinds of ill-posedness affect reconstruction quality (Section 4.1.2). Together, these two evaluations establish that the proposed method achieves competitive reconstruction quality across the range of CT acquisition conditions in DM4CT.

4.1.1 Quantitative Benchmark Comparison

We follow the standard DM4CT benchmark configurations to enable direct comparison with existing CT reconstruction methods. The five configurations are: (i) 40 projections without noise, (ii) 20 projection angles with mild noise, (iii) 80 projections with higher noise, (iv) 80 projections with mild noise and ring artifacts, and (v) 40 projections with limited-angle views [0,34​π][0,\frac{3}{4}\pi]. All methods are evaluated under the same forward operator, preprocessing, and metric computation protocol as DM4CT for fair comparison.

We compare the proposed method with representative approaches from multiple categories as in the DM4CT paper: Classical methods: filtered back projection (FBP) [26], simultaneous iterative reconstruction technique (SIRT) [14], and total variation (TV)-regularized reconstruction [41]. Unsupervised methods: deep image prior (DIP) [53] and implicit neural representations (INR) [42]. Supervised methods: a state-of-the-art supervised reconstruction network trained on paired data [31]. Diffusion-based methods: representative posterior sampling and data-consistency strategies, including DDS [8], DPS [7], PGDM [45], and ReSample [43].

Table 2 reports PSNR and SSIM for all methods included in the DM4CT benchmark [40] under all five standard configurations, evaluated on the full test set of 526 images. Baseline results are taken directly from DM4CT; results for the proposed method are produced under the same evaluation protocol using N=10N=10 stochastic reconstructions averaged to form the sample-mean reconstruction.

Evaluation protocol.

Our method generates multiple samples from the posterior distribution p⁡(x∣y)p(x\mid y), while some baseline methods produce a single deterministic reconstruction. For a fair quantitative comparison with deterministic benchmarks, we use the posterior mean reconstruction as the representative estimate. We generate NN reconstructions {xj(i)}i=1N\{x_{j}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} for test image jj and use their sample mean as the representative reconstruction:

x¯j:=1N​∑i=1Nxj(i)≈𝔼⁡[x∣yj].\bar{x}_{j}\;:=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{j}^{(i)}\;\approx\;\mathbb{E}[x\mid y_{j}]. (56)

The posterior mean is the minimum mean-squared-error estimator and provides a single reconstruction for comparison with deterministic methods. PSNR and SSIM are computed between x¯j\bar{x}_{j} and the corresponding ground-truth image xgt,jx_{\mathrm{gt},j}. We report the dataset averages

PSNRdataset=1M​∑j=1MPSNR⁡(x¯j,xgt,j),SSIMdataset=1M​∑j=1MSSIM⁡(x¯j,xgt,j),\operatorname{PSNR}_{\mathrm{dataset}}\;=\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\operatorname{PSNR}(\bar{x}_{j},x_{\mathrm{gt},j}),\qquad\operatorname{SSIM}_{\mathrm{dataset}}\;=\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\operatorname{SSIM}(\bar{x}_{j},x_{\mathrm{gt},j}), (57)

where M=526M=526 is the number of test images, and N=10N=10 is the number of samples.

For the noise-free and limited-angle settings (Configs i and v), the proposed method achieves the best performance among all compared methods. In Config i, it obtains 34.04 dB/0.89, outperforming the strongest unsupervised baseline, INR, by 0.83 dB, the strongest supervised restoration baseline, SwinIR, by 1.59 dB, and the strongest diffusion-based posterior baseline, ReSample, by 2.01 dB. The advantage is even larger in Config v, where the proposed method reaches 33.82 dB/0.88, exceeding the next-best method, INR, by 2.81 dB and 0.07 in SSIM.

This increase in margin from Config i to Config v is consistent with the role of geometry-aware guidance. In the sparse-view setting, the null-space is induced by missing views but is less directionally structured, so the advantage of geometry-aware comes primarily from the pullback metric redirecting updates away from measurement-sensitive directions. In the limited-angle setting, the null-space is strongly anisotropic and aligned with the missing angular range. The pullback metric explicitly accounts for this geometry, providing a stronger advantage as the null-space becomes more geometrically structured. This is also reflected in the behavior of ReSample, which drops from 32.03 dB in Config i to 27.70 dB in Config v, indicating that hard projection alone is insufficient for structured null-spaces.

For the noisy sparse-view settings, the proposed method remains competitive and is particularly strong among posterior-sampling methods. In Config ii, it achieves 28.98 dB/0.81 SSIM, outperforming DPS, DDS, PGDM, and ReSample. In Config iii, the acquisition contains more projection views but a higher noise level. The increased angular coverage reduces the geometric ambiguity and therefore limits the relative advantage of null-space-aware sampling. Reconstruction quality is instead determined mainly by the balance between noise suppression and measurement consistency. In addition, the effective measurement precision is based on a post-log Gaussian approximation that is most reliable at moderate-to-high photon counts. Under the stronger noise in Config iii, deviations from this approximation may lead to less accurate likelihood weighting and reduce reconstruction performance. Consequently, the proposed method obtains a slightly lower PSNR than MCG (28.83 versus 28.90 dB). However, it achieves substantially higher SSIM (0.80 versus 0.71), indicating better preservation of structural information.

Under ring artifacts (Config iv), the proposed method obtains 29.42 dB/0.81, giving one of the strongest structural reconstructions among diffusion-based methods. Resample is slightly higher in PSNR, while the proposed method maintains a higher SSIM. One possible explanation is that the projection-consistency term forces the reconstruction to match the measured sinogram. When the sinogram contains ring artifacts, this can also force the reconstruction to keep some of these artifacts, which may lower the PSNR. This suggests that ring artifacts may require artifact-aware noise modelling or adaptive precision weighting, so that unreliable sinogram components are not treated with the same confidence as clean measurements.

Since posterior-sampling methods are stochastic, their performance can depend on the particular sample drawn from the posterior. To assess this variability, we additionally generate 20 stochastic reconstruction samples for DDS, DPS, PGDM, ReSample, and the proposed method on one representative test slice for each acquisition configuration. We select DDS [8], DPS [7], PGDM [45], and ReSample [43] for this analysis because they achieve competitive performance in the benchmark and can generate multiple stochastic reconstruction samples. They therefore provide appropriate baselines for assessing both reconstruction accuracy and sampling variability. The posterior mean and sample variability are reported in Appendix B.1. This analysis is not intended to replace the benchmark-style comparison in Table 2, but to provide additional insight into the stability of the posterior samplers.

4.1.2 Qualitative Comparison across Acquisition Degradations

We compare visually against four representative diffusion-based methods: DDS [8], DPS [7], PGDM [45], and ReSample [43]. These methods represent two broad approaches to data consistency. DDS, DPS, and PGDM use gradient- or optimization-guided updates. ReSample combines a hard data-consistency correction with resampling. All four are top-performing diffusion-based methods in the DM4CT benchmark, making them strong and representative baselines. FBP is included as an analytical reference to the reconstruction difficulty of each setting rather than as a competitive baseline.

For comparison, we use a controlled configuration set that varies one factor at a time: (i) 40 projections without noise, (ii) 40 projections with mild Poisson noise, (iii) 40 projections with limited angular range [0,3​π/4][0,3\pi/4], (iv) 40 projections with limited angular range [0,π/2][0,\pi/2], and (v) 10 projections with mild Poisson noise. This isolates whether reconstruction degradation is caused by an enlarged null-space, missing directional information, or measurement noise. Figure 1 presents the qualitative results for all five settings.

As expected, FBP degrades rapidly as the inverse problem becomes more ill-posed. In the noise-free sparse-view setting (i), streak artifacts are already visible, and the cyan zoom shows a grid-like interference pattern with reduced cortical bone definition. Under mild Poisson noise (ii), noise amplification dominates the reconstruction, obscuring both the lung boundary and the vertebral structure. In the limited-angle settings (iii–iv), FBP exhibits directional blurring and streaking aligned with the missing angular range; this effect becomes stronger as the angular coverage is reduced from [0,3​π/4][0,3\pi/4] to [0,π/2][0,\pi/2]. The most severe degradation occurs in the highly sparse noisy case (v), where streak artifacts dominate the image and fine anatomy is largely lost.11 1 In the benchmark-compatible implementation, the angular grid includes both 00 and π\pi. For parallel-beam CT, these two views are redundant up to detector reversal, effectively leaving one fewer distinct projection direction. We keep this geometry unchanged for all methods to ensure a fair comparison.

The diffusion-based baselines show different behaviour across the five acquisition settings. DDS performs well when the measurements are noise-free: in setting (i), it recovers clean anatomy and sharp local structure (31.61 dB, SSIM 0.887), and it remains competitive in the limited-angle settings (iii–iv). However, it is much less robust to measurement noise. In the mild Poisson case (ii), its performance drops to 23.13 dB/0.342, with strong noise patterns in the lung region and a clear loss of vertebral structure in the cyan zoom. DPS and PGDM are more stable under noise, achieving 28.73 dB/0.802 and 28.28 dB/0.795 in setting (ii), respectively. However, their zoomed regions show residual smoothing and less distinct boundary detail, especially in the limited-angle cases. ReSample performs strongly in the sparse-view settings, reaching 32.32 dB/0.872 in setting (i) and 29.21 dB/0.780 in setting (ii), but degrades more substantially when the angular range is restricted. In setting (iv), it drops to 25.27 dB/0.768, and the zoomed regions show clear directional blurring. This suggests that hard projection is effective for sparse-view consistency, but is less sufficient when the null-space is structured by limited angular coverage.

The proposed method gives the strongest overall performance in the first four settings. It achieves 33.32 dB/0.897 in setting (i), 29.84 dB/0.846 in setting (ii), 33.19 dB/0.893 in setting (iii), and 29.17 dB/0.843 in setting (iv), giving the best PSNR and SSIM in each of these cases. These quantitative gains are consistent with the visual comparison: the proposed method better suppresses noise amplification, reduces directional artifacts, and preserves sharper anatomical boundaries in both zoomed regions. The advantage is particularly clear in the limited-angle setting (iii), where the proposed method outperforms the strongest competing posterior baseline, DDS, by 1.86 dB and produces sharper local structure in the vertebral zoom. This trend remains visible in the more severe limited-angle setting (iv). Although the margin is smaller, the proposed method still achieves the best PSNR and SSIM among the posterior methods, reaching 29.17 dB/0.843.

The most challenging setting (v), with only 10 noisy projections, shows a different trade-off. DPS obtains a slightly higher PSNR than the proposed method (27.42 dB versus 27.26 dB), but the proposed method achieves the highest SSIM among the posterior methods (0.786). Visually, DPS retains slightly more pixelwise contrast, but also shows residual streak artifacts, whereas the proposed method produces a smoother and more coherent reconstruction. This indicates that, in the most severely ill-posed noisy setting, PSNR and SSIM emphasise different aspects of reconstruction quality. In setting (v), the measurements are both extremely sparse and noisy. Under such conditions, hard or near-hard consistency, as used by ReSample and the proposed method, can preserve noise-related errors from the sinogram. This may limit PSNR, while the posterior mean still improves structural consistency, leading to high SSIM values.

Overall, the visual and quantitative results support the benefit of geometry-aware sampling. The measurement-consistency step stabilises the range-space component of the reconstruction, while the pullback-metric-guided diffusion update improves the weakly constrained directions where the learned prior is most useful. This combination helps reduce streak artifacts, preserve anatomical boundaries, and produce stable posterior-mean reconstructions across sparse-view, noisy, and limited-angle settings.

4.2 Empirical Sample-Variability Analysis

A key output of the proposed framework is empirical sample variability alongside the reconstruction. Figure 2 summarises this behaviour across the five acquisition settings (as in Section 4.1.2). For each configuration, we show the FBP reconstruction, the sample-mean reconstruction, the pixel-wise sample standard deviation, and the absolute error |x¯−xgt||\bar{x}-x_{\mathrm{gt}}|. This layout allows us to compare where the generated reconstructions vary with where the sample mean makes reconstruction errors.

In the noise-free sparse-view setting (i), the sample mean is close to the ground truth and the pixel-wise sample standard deviation is low across most of the image. The remaining sample variability is concentrated mainly around anatomical boundaries and fine structures. The absolute-error map shows a similar spatial pattern, with small errors in homogeneous regions and larger errors near interfaces. This suggests that, when the measurements are reliable, the generated reconstructions vary little in well-constrained regions and more near ambiguous structures.

Adding Poisson noise in setting (ii) substantially increases the pixel-wise sample standard deviation. Unlike the noise-free case, the variability is no longer confined mainly to edges, but spreads through the lung parenchyma and soft tissue. This reflects the fact that the measurements themselves are corrupted, so even geometrically observed directions are less reliable. The absolute-error map is also more widespread, while the sample mean remains visually much cleaner than the FBP reconstruction. This indicates that averaging over stochastic reconstructions suppresses much of the noise, while their variability still reflects the effect of noisy measurements.

The limited-angle settings show a different variability structure. In setting (iii), with angular range [0,3​π/4][0,3\pi/4], the pixel-wise sample standard deviation remains relatively low and is mainly visible around boundaries. In setting (iv), where the angular range is further reduced to [0,π/2][0,\pi/2], the variability becomes more pronounced and spatially structured, especially near the body boundary and along directions affected by the missing angular range. The corresponding error maps follow the same trend. In setting (iii), most errors appear near anatomical boundaries. In setting (iv), the errors become stronger and more directional. This suggests that the sample variability is related to the missing-angle geometry, rather than becoming uniformly larger across the image.

The most challenging case is setting (v), which combines only 10 projections with measurement noise. Here the pixel-wise sample standard deviation is high and spatially structured, with strong variability around the body boundary, lung region, and internal anatomical interfaces. The absolute-error map is also brightest in these regions. Compared with setting (ii), the variability is less uniformly diffuse and more strongly shaped by the acquisition geometry. This is consistent with the large null space induced by extreme view sparsity. Many image structures are weakly constrained by the measurements, while the data-consistency correction still promotes agreement with the measured projection directions.

The values in Table 3 are consistent with these observations. The proposed method gives the lowest mean pixel-wise sample standard deviation in the more informative settings: 0.0079 in Config i, 0.0081 in Config iii, and 0.0082 in Config iv. These low values indicate that the generated reconstructions agree closely when the measurements provide strong geometric constraints. In the noisy or highly undersampled settings, the variability increases, reaching 0.0260 in Config ii and 0.0205 in Config v. This increase is expected, since measurement noise and extreme view sparsity both enlarge the set of plausible reconstructions.

The corresponding spatial standard-deviation maps are shown in Appendix B.2, Figure 7. Compared with the diffusion-based baselines, the proposed method generally produces lower variability across reconstructions.
