DDS, DPS, and PGDM have higher mean pixel-wise standard deviations in most configurations. ReSample gives the closest competing values: its variability is higher than that of the proposed method in Configs i, iii, iv, and v, but lower in Config ii (0.0182 versus 0.0260). Lower variability alone does not necessarily indicate better uncertainty estimation, since it may also result from insufficient exploration. In our results, however, the proposed method combines competitive reconstruction quality with spatial variability that corresponds to anatomical interfaces, noisy regions, and structures affected by missing views. This correspondence suggests that the maps capture measurement-related reconstruction ambiguity rather than only uncontrolled sampling variation. They remain empirical variability diagnostics rather than calibrated posterior-uncertainty estimates.

4.3 Geometry-aware analysis

The previous sections evaluated reconstruction quality using PSNR and SSIM (Section 4.1) and characterised empirical sample variability through standard-deviation maps (Section 4.2). While these results quantify reconstruction fidelity and show where the generated reconstructions vary, they do not fully explain how the acquisition geometry shapes the reconstructions or their variability. To provide this geometric perspective, we next perform a geometry-aware analysis using regularized range–null component diagnostics.

First, we validate the regularized range–null component analysis on representative reconstructions and confirm that the extracted null-like component is effectively invisible to the measurement operator (Section 4.3.1). Second, we apply the decomposition to stochastic reconstructions and examine whether their sample variability is concentrated in approximately measurement-invisible directions, as predicted by the geometry of the method (Section 4.3.2). Third, we isolate the role of pullback-metric preconditioning by comparing the proposed update with a Euclidean drift baseline, verifying that the geometry-aware update preferentially moves along weakly constrained directions while maintaining measurement consistency (Section 4.3.3). Finally, we evaluate the effect of signal-dependent precision weighting derived from the Poisson photon-counting noise model and demonstrate its benefit under realistic CT noise (Section 4.3.4).

4.3.1 Regularized Range–Null Component Analysis

Before analysing variability across stochastic reconstructions, we examine how the sample-mean reconstruction separates into measurement-sensitive and weakly constrained components. This analysis is motivated by the exact orthogonal direct-sum structure in Proposition 1, but avoids explicitly computing a pseudoinverse.

We define the regularized range-component operator

PR,γdec:=AΩ⊤​(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γdec​Im)−1​AΩ,γdec>0,P_{R,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}\;:=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\left(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}I_{m}\right)^{-1}A_{\Omega},\qquad\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}>0, (58)

and its complementary null-like component operator

PN,γdec:=In−PR,γdec.P_{N,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}\;:=\;I_{n}-P_{R,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}. (59)

Because the exact range–null decomposition is determined by AΩA_{\Omega}, we use the unweighted Euclidean operator in this diagnostic. This isolates the effect of the acquisition geometry from the noise weighting used during reconstruction.

For a reconstruction xx, we define

xrange:=PR,γdec​x,xnull:=PN,γdec​x.x_{\mathrm{range}}\;:=\;P_{R,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}x,\qquad x_{\mathrm{null}}\;:=\;P_{N,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}x. (60)

By construction,

x=xrange+xnull.x=x_{\mathrm{range}}+x_{\mathrm{null}}. (61)

Here, γdec>0\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}>0 is a diagnostic regularization parameter used only for this post-processing analysis. It stabilizes the measurement-space solve and controls how strongly weakly observed directions are assigned to the null-like component. Smaller values produce a closer approximation to the exact range–null decomposition but lead to a more ill-conditioned linear system.

The component xrangex_{\mathrm{range}} lies in ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) because it has the form AΩ⊤​qA_{\Omega}^{\top}q for some q∈ℝmq\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. It therefore emphasizes directions that affect the measured sinogram. The complementary component xnullx_{\mathrm{null}} emphasizes directions that are weakly constrained or unobservable under the acquisition geometry.

For finite γdec>0\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}>0, these operators are regularized component operators rather than exact orthogonal projectors. Consequently, xnullx_{\mathrm{null}} need not lie exactly in 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}), and the two components need not be orthogonal. As γdec→0\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}\to 0, the operators approach the orthogonal projectors onto ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) and 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}), respectively.

To make the regularization independent of the numerical scaling of AΩA_{\Omega}, we set

γdec=η​λmax​(AΩ​AΩ⊤),η=10−4.\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}\;=\;\eta\,\lambda_{\max}\left(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\right),\qquad\eta=10^{-4}. (62)

The largest eigenvalue is estimated using 20 matrix-free power iterations. For the 40-projection geometry used here, this gives λmax​(AΩ​AΩ⊤)≈1.9606×104\lambda_{\max}(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top})\approx 1.9606\times 10^{4} and γdec≈1.9606\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}\approx 1.9606. The linear systems are solved by conjugate gradient with relative tolerance 10−610^{-6}.

We quantify the relative squared norms of the two components and their cross term by

rrange=‖xrange‖22‖x‖22,rnull=‖xnull‖22‖x‖22,ccross=2​⟨xrange,xnull⟩‖x‖22.r_{\mathrm{range}}\;=\;\frac{\|x_{\mathrm{range}}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|x\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad r_{\mathrm{null}}\;=\;\frac{\|x_{\mathrm{null}}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|x\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{cross}}\;=\;\frac{2\langle x_{\mathrm{range}},x_{\mathrm{null}}\rangle}{\|x\|_{2}^{2}}. (63)

These quantities satisfy

rrange+rnull+ccross=1.r_{\mathrm{range}}+r_{\mathrm{null}}+c_{\mathrm{cross}}=1. (64)

Because ccrossc_{\mathrm{cross}} is generally nonzero, the first two quantities are relative component-magnitude diagnostics rather than fractions of an orthogonal energy decomposition.

We further measure the relative sinogram response of the null-like component:

ρnull=‖AΩ​xnull‖2‖AΩ​x‖2.\rho_{\mathrm{null}}\;=\;\frac{\|A_{\Omega}x_{\mathrm{null}}\|_{2}}{\|A_{\Omega}x\|_{2}}. (65)

A small value of ρnull\rho_{\mathrm{null}} indicates that the extracted null-like component only weakly affects the predicted sinogram.

Figure 3 shows that the regularized range component retains most of the overall image magnitude and low-frequency anatomical content, whereas the null-like component emphasizes edge- and streak-like structures that are weakly constrained by the acquisition geometry. Quantitatively, the range-component squared norm is 99.631%99.631\% of the reconstruction squared norm in the noise-free case and 99.729%99.729\% in the Poisson-noise case. The corresponding null-like-component ratios are 0.305%0.305\% and 0.217%0.217\%, respectively.

In both settings, ρnull\rho_{\mathrm{null}} is below 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, showing that the extracted null-like component has only a small effect on the sinogram. These results support its interpretation as an approximately measurement-invisible component under the 40-projection geometry. Because this experiment analyses posterior means, the component ratios should not be interpreted as measures of posterior uncertainty; variability across stochastic reconstruction samples is examined separately.

4.3.2 Geometry-Aware Posterior Variability Analysis

We next analyse the geometry of the posterior variability produced by the proposed reconstruction method. For each acquisition setting, we first generate KK posterior reconstructions {x(k)}k=1K\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} of the same test image using different random seeds and the same measured sinogram. The posterior mean is then computed as x¯=1K​∑k=1Kx(k)\bar{x}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}x^{(k)}. All diagnostics in this subsection are computed from these reconstructed stochastic reconstruction samples. Thus, the analysis does not study synthetic perturbations, but the actual variability of the reconstructions produced by the sampler.

To investigate whether this posterior variability follows the measurement geometry, we perform two complementary analyses. First, we compare the variability of the posterior reconstructions in image space with their variability after applying the CT forward operator. Given the stochastic reconstruction samples {x(k)}k=1K\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} and sample mean x¯\bar{x}, we compute

σx\displaystyle\sigma_{x} =1K​∑k=1K(x(k)−x¯)2,σy\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(x^{(k)}-\bar{x}\right)^{2}},\qquad\sigma_{y} =1K​∑k=1K(AΩ​x(k)−AΩ​x¯)2.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(A_{\Omega}x^{(k)}-A_{\Omega}\bar{x}\right)^{2}}. (66)

Here, σx\sigma_{x} measures pixel-wise variability across reconstructed images, whereas σy\sigma_{y} measures how much this variability remains visible in the corresponding sinograms.

To compare variability in the two domains, we normalise by the magnitude of the corresponding posterior mean:

Rimg\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{img}} =‖σx‖2‖x¯‖2,Rsino\displaystyle=\frac{\|\sigma_{x}\|_{2}}{\|\bar{x}\|_{2}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{sino}} =‖σy‖2‖AΩ​x¯‖2,Rsino/img\displaystyle=\frac{\|\sigma_{y}\|_{2}}{\|A_{\Omega}\bar{x}\|_{2}},\qquad R_{\mathrm{sino/img}} =RsinoRimg.\displaystyle=\frac{R_{\mathrm{sino}}}{R_{\mathrm{img}}}. (67)

A small value of Rsino/imgR_{\mathrm{sino/img}} means that differences between posterior reconstructions are strongly reduced after applying the forward operator. This indicates that much of the image-space variability lies in directions that are weakly visible, or approximately invisible, to the measurements.

Second, we decompose the deviation of each posterior reconstruction from the posterior mean,

v(k)=x(k)−x¯v^{(k)}=x^{(k)}-\bar{x} (68)

into a measurement-visible component and an approximately measurement-invisible component:

vrange(k)=PR,γdec​v(k),vnull(k)=PN,γdec​v(k).v_{\mathrm{range}}^{(k)}\;=\;P_{R,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}v^{(k)},\qquad v_{\mathrm{null}}^{(k)}\;=\;P_{N,\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}}v^{(k)}. (69)

The relative contributions of the two components are quantified by

rrange(k)\displaystyle r_{\mathrm{range}}^{(k)} =‖vrange(k)‖22‖v(k)‖22,rnull(k)\displaystyle=\;\frac{\|v_{\mathrm{range}}^{(k)}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|v^{(k)}\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad r_{\mathrm{null}}^{(k)} =‖vnull(k)‖22‖v(k)‖22.\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{\|v_{\mathrm{null}}^{(k)}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|v^{(k)}\|_{2}^{2}}. (70)

The quantities rrange(k)r_{\mathrm{range}}^{(k)} and rnull(k)r_{\mathrm{null}}^{(k)} measure the relative energy of the measurement-visible and approximately measurement-invisible components of each posterior deviation. Since the projection is computed with a finite regularisation parameter γdec\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}, these values should be interpreted as diagnostic energy ratios rather than exact orthogonal fractions.

While Rsino/imgR_{\mathrm{sino/img}} measures the overall suppression of posterior variability after applying the forward operator, the quantities rranger_{\mathrm{range}} and rnullr_{\mathrm{null}} describe how the image-space posterior deviations are distributed between measurement-visible and approximately measurement-invisible components. Together, these diagnostics show both how strongly the stochastic reconstruction samples remain constrained by the measurements and where the remaining variability is concentrated.

Table 5 summarises the geometry-aware posterior variability diagnostics from two complementary perspectives. First, the ratios RimgR_{\mathrm{img}}, RsinoR_{\mathrm{sino}}, and Rsino/imgR_{\mathrm{sino/img}} compare the variability of posterior reconstructions in image space with the variability that remains after applying the CT forward operator. Second, the range–null diagnostic ratios r¯range\bar{r}_{\mathrm{range}} and r¯null\bar{r}_{\mathrm{null}} describe whether the image-space posterior deviations are mainly measurement-visible or approximately measurement-invisible.

From the measurement-space perspective, all three settings show much smaller variability in sinogram space than in image space. This indicates that although the stochastic reconstruction samples differ visibly as reconstructed images, these differences are strongly reduced after applying the measurement operator. The strongest suppression occurs in the 40-projection noise-free setting, where Rsino/img=0.0399R_{\mathrm{sino/img}}=0.0399, meaning that the relative variability in measurement space is only about 4%4\% of that in image space. With Poisson noise, this ratio increases to 0.27370.2737 for 40 projections. With both Poisson noise and stronger undersampling, it further increases to 0.30430.3043 for 20 projections. This trend is consistent with the measurements becoming less informative: noise reduces the reliability of the measured sinogram, and fewer projection angles leave more image directions weakly constrained.

The range–null diagnostics provide a complementary view of the same behaviour. In the 40-projection noise-free setting, the posterior deviations are dominated by the approximately measurement-invisible component (r¯null=1.046\bar{r}_{\mathrm{null}}=1.046 versus r¯range=0.184\bar{r}_{\mathrm{range}}=0.184; their sum exceeds one because the cross-term c¯cross≈−0.23\bar{c}_{\mathrm{cross}}\approx-0.23 is nonzero for finite γdec\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}). This indicates that, once measurement consistency is enforced, the remaining posterior variability lies mainly in directions that have little effect on the measured sinogram. Under Poisson noise, the measurement-visible contribution increases (r¯range=0.422\bar{r}_{\mathrm{range}}=0.422), reflecting the fact that uncertainty in the measurements can also produce variability in directions visible to the forward operator. Nevertheless, the approximately null component remains larger (r¯null=0.618\bar{r}_{\mathrm{null}}=0.618). In the 20-projection noisy case, the null component again dominates (r¯null=0.697\bar{r}_{\mathrm{null}}=0.697), consistent with the larger null-space induced by stronger angular undersampling.

Overall, the two diagnostics give consistent evidence that the proposed sampler produces geometry-aware posterior variability. The stochastic reconstruction samples differ primarily in image directions that are weakly constrained by the acquisition, while remaining comparatively consistent in the measurement domain.

4.3.3 Effect of Pullback-Metric Preconditioning

To isolate the effect of pullback-metric preconditioning, we compare the proposed deterministic update with an identical Euclidean update. Within each acquisition geometry, the two variants use the same pretrained prior, data-fidelity term, initialization, reconstruction parameters, and regularized data-consistency schedule. Langevin noise and the additional approximately null-space-restricted perturbation are disabled in both cases. We consider two noise-free configurations with the same number of measurements: 40-view full-angle CT over [0,π][0,\pi] and 40-view limited-angle CT over [0,3​π/4][0,3\pi/4]. The endpoint convention matches the DM4CT benchmark geometry.

At reconstruction iteration kk, let s(k)s^{(k)} denote the DDPM score estimate evaluated at the corresponding noised image state. We form the combined guidance direction

r(k)=λk​s(k)−μk​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x(k)−y).r^{(k)}\;=\;\lambda_{k}s^{(k)}-\mu_{k}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\left(A_{\Omega}x^{(k)}-y\right). (71)

This is the practical annealed guidance direction used by the implementation, rather than the exact score of the clean-image posterior. The Euclidean variant applies

uEuc(k)=r(k),u_{\mathrm{Euc}}^{(k)}\;=\;r^{(k)}, (72)

whereas the pullback-preconditioned variant solves

(AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​In)​ugeo(k)=r(k).\left(A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n}\right)u_{\mathrm{geo}}^{(k)}\;=\;r^{(k)}. (73)

Thus, within each geometry, the variants differ only in whether the combined guidance is preconditioned by Gγ=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​InG_{\gamma}=A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n}.

Figure 4 shows that pullback preconditioning improves reconstruction quality in both geometries. For full-angle CT, PSNR increases from 31.9831.98 to 33.1733.17 dB and SSIM increases from 0.83390.8339 to 0.88520.8852. For limited-angle CT, PSNR increases from 31.6331.63 to 33.0433.04 dB and SSIM increases from 0.83590.8359 to 0.88160.8816. In the yellow region, the pullback-preconditioned reconstructions preserve the lung–soft-tissue interface more clearly. In the cyan region, they recover a sharper and more continuous vertebral boundary. Compared with the Euclidean variant, the pullback-preconditioned results also exhibit less local blurring and fewer residual streak artifacts. These visual differences are consistent with the improvements in PSNR and SSIM.

We quantify agreement with the measured sinogram using

RelErry=‖AΩ​x−y‖2‖y‖2.\mathrm{RelErr}_{y}\;=\;\frac{\|A_{\Omega}x-y\|_{2}}{\|y\|_{2}}. (74)

To examine the geometry of the applied drift, let Δ​xdet(k)\Delta x_{\mathrm{det}}^{(k)} denote the deterministic displacement before Langevin noise, null-space perturbation, and the subsequent data-consistency correction. We define

ρΔ​x(k)=‖AΩ​Δ​xdet(k)‖2‖Δ​xdet(k)‖2,\rho_{\Delta x}^{(k)}\;=\;\frac{\|A_{\Omega}\Delta x_{\mathrm{det}}^{(k)}\|_{2}}{\|\Delta x_{\mathrm{det}}^{(k)}\|_{2}}, (75)

and report

ρ¯Δ​x=1T​∑k=0T−1ρΔ​x(k).\bar{\rho}_{\Delta x}\;=\;\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\rho_{\Delta x}^{(k)}. (76)

This quantity measures the sinogram change per unit image-space displacement. A smaller value indicates a displacement with lower measurement sensitivity.

As shown in Table 6, pullback preconditioning improves PSNR by 1.191.19 dB in the full-angle case and 1.411.41 dB in the limited-angle case. The Euclidean variant gives the smaller relative data error, but all four errors remain below 2.3×10−42.3\times 10^{-4}. Although the pullback variant does not attain the lowest measurement residual, it maintains strong measurement agreement, with RelErry<2.3×10−4\mathrm{RelErr}_{y}<2.3\times 10^{-4}, while substantially improving PSNR and SSIM.

The update-response diagnostic changes much more strongly. In the full-angle case, ρ¯Δ​x\bar{\rho}_{\Delta x} decreases from 1.04×1021.04\times 10^{2} to 3.96×10−13.96\times 10^{-1}, a reduction by a factor of approximately 263263. In the limited-angle case, it decreases from 1.10×1021.10\times 10^{2} to 2.89×10−12.89\times 10^{-1}, a reduction by a factor of approximately 381381. These results show that the pullback metric substantially reduces the measurement response of the applied deterministic displacement. Together with the range–null diagnostic below, this is consistent with shifting the update toward more weakly constrained image directions.

For the component diagnostic, define

B:=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ.B\;:=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}. (77)

For each sampled displacement Δ​xdet(k)\Delta x_{\mathrm{det}}^{(k)}, we compute

Δ​xR(k)=(B+γdec​In)−1​B​Δ​xdet(k),Δ​xN(k)=Δ​xdet(k)−Δ​xR(k).\Delta x_{R}^{(k)}\;=\;\left(B+\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}I_{n}\right)^{-1}B\Delta x_{\mathrm{det}}^{(k)},\qquad\Delta x_{N}^{(k)}\;=\;\Delta x_{\mathrm{det}}^{(k)}-\Delta x_{R}^{(k)}. (78)

Here γdec>0\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}>0 regularizes the matrix-free CG solve. For finite γdec\gamma_{\mathrm{dec}}, Δ​xN(k)\Delta x_{N}^{(k)} is a null-like component rather than an exact element of 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}), and the two components need not be orthogonal. We therefore use the squared component-magnitude ratio

rN(k)rR(k)=‖Δ​xN(k)‖22‖Δ​xR(k)‖22\frac{r_{N}^{(k)}}{r_{R}^{(k)}}\;=\;\frac{\|\Delta x_{N}^{(k)}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\Delta x_{R}^{(k)}\|_{2}^{2}} (79)

as a diagnostic rather than as an exact partition of image energy.

Figure 5 shows the evolution of the update response and the regularized component ratio. The Euclidean displacement has a substantially larger measurement response, whereas pullback preconditioning keeps this response much smaller over the reconstruction trajectory. The component ratio provides a complementary interpretation: a larger null-like-to-range ratio indicates that relatively more of the applied displacement lies along weakly constrained or unobservable directions.

Figure 5 shows that pullback preconditioning changes the geometry of the applied deterministic displacement throughout reconstruction. In both acquisition settings, the Euclidean displacement remains strongly measurement-sensitive, with ρΔ​x(k)\rho_{\Delta x}^{(k)} generally of order 10210^{2}. After the initial iteration, pullback preconditioning reduces this response to approximately 10−110^{-1}–10010^{0}. The regularized component analysis gives a complementary result. The null-like-to-range ratio remains below one for the Euclidean variant, whereas it rises well above one for the pullback variant and remains large over most of the trajectory. These observations indicate that pullback preconditioning suppresses displacement components that strongly affect the measured sinogram while retaining relatively more movement along weakly constrained and unobservable directions.

Taken together, the reconstruction metrics, measurement residuals, and update diagnostics show that pullback preconditioning changes the deterministic update in a manner consistent with the measurement geometry. It reduces movement that strongly affects the measured sinogram and permits relatively larger movement along weakly constrained directions, where the learned prior can contribute anatomical information. In these experiments, this change is associated with improved PSNR and SSIM while the final measurement residual remains small.

4.3.4 Effect of Signal-Dependent Precision Weighting

We finally examine the effect of the signal-dependent precision weighting used in the proposed method. In the Poisson photon-counting model of CT, different sinogram entries have different noise levels: rays with lower photon counts are less reliable than rays with higher photon counts. Following the Gaussian approximation described in Section 3.6 and Appendix A.1, we model this using a signal-dependent covariance

Σ^−1=diag⁡(w1,…,wm),\widehat{\Sigma}^{-1}\;=\;\operatorname{diag}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}), (80)

where wi>0w_{i}>0 is a stabilized approximation of the estimated photon count λ^i=I0​e−yi\widehat{\lambda}_{i}=I_{0}e^{-y_{i}} for the ii-th sinogram entry; the precise construction is given in Appendix A.1.

This signal-dependent covariance enters the proposed method in three places. First, it appears in the weighted data-fidelity term

Φ(x)=12‖Σ^−1/2(AΩx−y)‖22.\Phi(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\left\|\widehat{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right\|_{2}^{2}. (81)

Second, it appears in the pullback metric

Gγ=AΩ⊤​Σ^−1​AΩ+γ​I.G_{\gamma}\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\widehat{\Sigma}^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I. (82)

Third, the same metric defines the geometry-aware Langevin perturbation,

νG(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,2​αk​Gγ−1).\nu_{G}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,2\alpha_{k}G_{\gamma}^{-1}\right). (83)

In practice, this noise sampler is implemented in a matrix-free way: GγG_{\gamma} is never formed explicitly, and only matrix-vector products

Gγ​v=AΩ⊤​Σ^−1​AΩ​v+γ​vG_{\gamma}v\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\widehat{\Sigma}^{-1}A_{\Omega}v+\gamma v (84)

are required.

To isolate the contribution of this signal-dependent weighting, we compare the full method against an ablation in which Σ^\widehat{\Sigma} is replaced by the identity matrix. This unit-precision variant treats all sinogram bins as equally reliable.

Both variants use the same pretrained diffusion prior, pullback-metric preconditioning, projection step, initialization, and hyperparameters. The only difference is whether the method uses the physically motivated signal-dependent covariance Σ^\widehat{\Sigma} or the unit covariance II. We evaluate the two variants under three 40-projection settings: no noise, Gaussian noise, and Poisson noise. The Poisson setting is the case where signal-dependent weighting is expected to matter most.

Figure 6 shows that signal-dependent precision has little effect when the measurement noise is absent or spatially uniform. In the noise-free setting, the two variants of our method are identical, giving 33.32 dB/0.897. The same is true under Gaussian noise, where both variants achieve 31.62 dB/0.867. This is expected: when all sinogram entries have the same noise level, unit precision is an appropriate model.

The situation changes under Poisson noise. FBP is strongly corrupted by noise, and DDS also degrades substantially to 23.08 dB/0.339. DPS is more stable, reaching 28.62 dB/0.800. The unit-precision version of our method performs worse than DPS, with 28.23 dB/0.691. This shows that using the wrong noise model can reduce the benefit of the geometry-aware update: if all sinogram bins are treated as equally reliable, noisy low-photon-count measurements can be over-weighted.

With signal-dependent precision, the proposed method improves to 29.84 dB/0.846. This is a gain of 1.61 dB and 0.155 SSIM over the unit-precision variant, and it also outperforms DPS by 1.22 dB and 0.046 SSIM. The improvement is visible in the cyan zoomed region around the vertebral body. The unit-precision reconstruction contains stronger noise-driven artifacts and a less clear cortical bone boundary, whereas the signal-dependent reconstruction gives a cleaner and sharper structure.

This behaviour is consistent with the Poisson noise model. Rays passing through high-attenuation tissue, such as bone, produce fewer detected photons and therefore have higher measurement variance. The signal-dependent precision down-weights these less reliable measurements in both the data-fidelity term and the pullback metric. As a result, the reconstruction is less dominated by noisy sinogram entries and relies more appropriately on the learned prior in uncertain regions.

These results show that signal-dependent precision is important for realistic Poisson CT noise. At the same time, it is complementary to the geometry-aware part of the method. In the noise-free and Gaussian-noise settings, where signal-dependent weighting provides no additional advantage, the proposed method already performs strongly. Under Poisson noise, the weighting becomes necessary to preserve this advantage by matching the data-consistency term to the physical noise model.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

We presented a geometry-aware posterior sampling method for sparse-view and limited-angle CT reconstruction. The method combines a diffusion prior with data consistency and a pullback-metric update. Instead of applying the diffusion update directly in image space, we use the measurement-induced metric GγG_{\gamma} to adapt the update direction to the CT acquisition geometry. This reduces updates that would strongly change the measured sinogram, while allowing the learned prior to act in directions that are weakly constrained by the measurements.

The experiments show that this geometry-aware design improves reconstruction quality across sparse-view, noisy, and limited-angle CT settings. The proposed method reduces streak artifacts, suppresses noise amplification, and preserves anatomical boundaries more clearly than the posterior-sampling baselines considered. The pullback update also improves PSNR and SSIM compared with the Euclidean update, while keeping the measurement residual very small. The update-direction analysis further shows that the pullback metric reduces the measurement response of the deterministic update and redirects it toward approximately measurement-invisible directions.

The method also provides posterior uncertainty estimates. The posterior mean gives the final reconstruction, while the empirical sample standard-deviation map shows where the reconstruction is uncertain. In our experiments, Uncertainty is highest near anatomical boundaries, fine structures, and noise-sensitive regions, as well as structures weakly constrained by missing angular coverage in limited-angle CT. These regions often coincide with larger reconstruction errors, suggesting that the maps capture reconstruction ambiguity. By showing which structures are less reliably determined by the measured data, the maps improve the interpretability of learned reconstructions in ambiguous inverse problems.

Several directions remain for future work. First, although we test Poisson-corrupted measurements, the current posterior model uses a Gaussian approximation to the CT noise model. This approximation is reasonable when photon counts are not too low, but it may become inaccurate in very low-dose CT. A natural extension is to use the Poisson likelihood more directly. In that case, the data-fidelity term and the pullback metric would depend on the predicted photon counts at the current reconstruction. This could give a more accurate uncertainty model in strongly noise-dominated settings.

Second, the current method requires iterative linear solves to apply the inverse pullback metric during the reverse process. This makes the method more expensive than a Euclidean update. Future work should therefore develop faster matrix-free methods for applying Gγ−1G_{\gamma}^{-1}. Possible directions include preconditioned conjugate gradients, warm-starting the solver across reverse iterations, adaptive stopping criteria, multigrid methods, low-rank approximations, and learned approximations of the inverse metric. Faster solvers would make the method easier to scale to larger images and three-dimensional CT volumes.

Finally, future work will consider latent-space versions of the method, to accelerate reconstruction speed, which would require a latent pullback metric.

Appendix A Theoretical Support

A.1 Gaussian Approximation of CT Measurements

This subsection motivates the approximate linear–Gaussian model

y=AΩ​x+ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),y=A_{\Omega}x+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),

used in the main text. The derivation starts from an idealized Poisson photon-counting model and explains the diagonal, signal-dependent covariance of the post-log measurements. It also describes the fixed plug-in precision used during reconstruction.

A.1.1 Poisson photon-counting model

Under a monoenergetic Beer–Lambert model, the expected photon count at detector bin ii is [58]

λi=I0​e−(AΩ​x)i,\lambda_{i}\;=\;I_{0}e^{-(A_{\Omega}x)_{i}}, (85)

where I0I_{0} is the incident photon count, x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the image of linear-attenuation coefficients, and (AΩ​x)i(A_{\Omega}x)_{i} is the line integral for ray ii. The detected count is modeled as

Yi∼Poisson⁡(λi),𝔼⁡[Yi]=λi,Var⁡(Yi)=λi.Y_{i}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{i}),\qquad\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]=\lambda_{i},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i})=\lambda_{i}. (86)

Thus, the variance of the raw count depends on its expected value.

This model is an idealization. Real CT measurements may additionally include electronic noise, scatter, beam hardening, detector correlations, and effects introduced by calibration and preprocessing [58, 59].

A.1.2 Gaussian approximation of Poisson counts

For a sufficiently large expected transmitted count, a Poisson random variable is well approximated by a Gaussian random variable with the same mean and variance.

Proposition 2 (Gaussian limit of the Poisson distribution).

Let Yλ∼Poisson⁡(λ)Y_{\lambda}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda) and define

Zλ:=Yλ−λλ.Z_{\lambda}\;:=\;\frac{Y_{\lambda}-\lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}}.

Then Zλ→𝑑𝒩⁡(0,1)Z_{\lambda}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,1) as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty.

Proof.

The moment-generating function of YλY_{\lambda} is

MYλ​(t)\displaystyle M_{Y_{\lambda}}(t) =𝔼⁡[et​Yλ]\displaystyle\;=\;\mathbb{E}[e^{tY_{\lambda}}]
=∑k=0∞et​k​λk​e−λk!\displaystyle\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{tk}\frac{\lambda^{k}e^{-\lambda}}{k!}
=exp⁡(λ⁡(et−1)).\displaystyle\;=\;\exp\!\left(\lambda(e^{t}-1)\right).

Consequently,

MZλ​(t)\displaystyle M_{Z_{\lambda}}(t) =e−t​λ​MYλ​(tλ)\displaystyle\;=\;e^{-t\sqrt{\lambda}}M_{Y_{\lambda}}\!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)
=exp⁡[−t​λ+λ⁡(et/λ−1)].\displaystyle\;=\;\exp\!\left[-t\sqrt{\lambda}+\lambda\left(e^{t/\sqrt{\lambda}}-1\right)\right].

For fixed tt,

et/λ= 1+tλ+t22​λ+O(λ−3/2),e^{t/\sqrt{\lambda}}\;=\;1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\lambda}}+\frac{t^{2}}{2\lambda}+O(\lambda^{-3/2}),

and therefore

MZλ(t)=exp(t22+O(λ−1/2))⟶exp(t22).M_{Z_{\lambda}}(t)\;=\;\exp\!\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}+O(\lambda^{-1/2})\right)\longrightarrow\exp\!\left(\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right).

The limiting function is the moment-generating function of 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). The continuity theorem for moment-generating functions then gives the convergence in distribution. ∎

Equivalently, for sufficiently large λ\lambda,

Yλ≈λ+λ​η,η∼𝒩⁡(0,1),Y_{\lambda}\approx\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda}\,\eta,\qquad\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),

or Yλ≈𝒩⁡(λ,λ)Y_{\lambda}\approx\mathcal{N}(\lambda,\lambda). The quality of this approximation depends on the transmitted count λ\lambda, rather than only on the incident count I0I_{0}. A highly attenuated ray can therefore remain in the low-count regime even when I0I_{0} is relatively large [58, 55].

A.1.3 Propagation through the logarithmic transform

Let Y~i>0\widetilde{Y}_{i}>0 denote the detected count after zero-count correction, and define the post-log measurement

yi:=−log⁡(Y~iI0).y_{i}\;:=\;-\log\!\left(\frac{\widetilde{Y}_{i}}{I_{0}}\right). (87)

For example, zero counts may be replaced using

Y~i=max⁡(Yi,Ymin),Ymin>0.\widetilde{Y}_{i}\;=\;\max(Y_{i},Y_{\min}),\qquad Y_{\min}>0.

This correction prevents infinite log-sinogram values. However, it modifies the count distribution and may introduce additional bias when the detected photon count is low [55].

To derive a local Gaussian approximation, we temporarily neglect count clipping and assume Y~i=Yi>0\widetilde{Y}_{i}=Y_{i}>0. Define

f⁡(u)=−log⁡(u/I0),f′​(u)=−1u,f′′​(u)=1u2.f(u)\;=\;-\log(u/I_{0}),\qquad f^{\prime}(u)\;=\;-\frac{1}{u},\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(u)\;=\;\frac{1}{u^{2}}.

Since

f⁡(λi)=−log⁡(λiI0)=(AΩ​x)i,f(\lambda_{i})\;=\;-\log\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{I_{0}}\right)\;=\;(A_{\Omega}x)_{i},

a first-order Taylor expansion of f⁡(Yi)f(Y_{i}) around λi\lambda_{i} gives

yi\displaystyle y_{i} ≈f⁡(λi)+f′​(λi)​(Yi−λi)\displaystyle\approx f(\lambda_{i})+f^{\prime}(\lambda_{i})(Y_{i}-\lambda_{i})
=(AΩ​x)i−Yi−λiλi.\displaystyle=(A_{\Omega}x)_{i}-\frac{Y_{i}-\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}}.

For sufficiently large λi\lambda_{i}, Proposition 2 gives

Yi−λi≈λi​ηi,ηi∼𝒩⁡(0,1).Y_{i}-\lambda_{i}\approx\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\,\eta_{i},\qquad\eta_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Therefore,

yi≈(AΩ​x)i−1λi​ηi.y_{i}\approx(A_{\Omega}x)_{i}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}}\eta_{i}. (88)

Because −ηi-\eta_{i} has the same distribution as ηi\eta_{i}, the leading post-log error is approximately Gaussian with zero mean and variance λi−1\lambda_{i}^{-1}.

The first-order approximation does not capture the bias introduced by the nonlinear logarithm. Retaining the quadratic term gives

𝔼⁡[yi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[y_{i}] ≈f⁡(λi)+12​f′′​(λi)​Var⁡(Yi)\displaystyle\approx f(\lambda_{i})+\frac{1}{2}f^{\prime\prime}(\lambda_{i})\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i})
=(AΩ​x)i+12​λi,\displaystyle=(A_{\Omega}x)_{i}+\frac{1}{2\lambda_{i}},

where Var⁡(Yi)=λi\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i})=\lambda_{i}. The post-log variance is approximately

Var⁡(yi)≈(f′​(λi))2​Var⁡(Yi)=1λi.\operatorname{Var}(y_{i})\;\approx\;\bigl(f^{\prime}(\lambda_{i})\bigr)^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i})\;=\;\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}}.

The zero-mean Gaussian model used below neglects the leading bias 1/(2​λi)1/(2\lambda_{i}). This approximation is most accurate when the transmitted photon count λi\lambda_{i} is sufficiently large.

A.1.4 Post-log covariance and likelihood

Under the additional approximation that detector-bin counts are conditionally independent, the post-log errors are approximately independent. Stacking the measurements gives

y≈AΩ​x+ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),Σ=diag⁡(1λ1,…,1λm).y\approx A_{\Omega}x+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),\qquad\Sigma\;=\;\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}},\ldots,\frac{1}{\lambda_{m}}\right). (89)

The term post-log indicates that this Gaussian model is applied after the logarithmic transformation of the photon counts [58, 55].

Using (85),

Var⁡(εi)≈1λi=exp⁡((AΩ​x)i)I0.\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{i})\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}}\;=\;\frac{\exp((A_{\Omega}x)_{i})}{I_{0}}.

Thus, highly attenuated rays receive lower precision. This motivates the post-log weighted least-squares functional [55, 61]

Φ(x)=12‖Σ−1/2(AΩx−y)‖22.\Phi(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right\|_{2}^{2}.

A.1.5 Fixed effective precision

The ideal post-log precision depends on the unknown transmitted count λi=I0​exp⁡[−(AΩ​x)i]\lambda_{i}=I_{0}\exp[-(A_{\Omega}x)_{i}]. An ideal count-based plug-in estimate would be

λ^i=I0​e−yi.\widehat{\lambda}_{i}\;=\;I_{0}e^{-y_{i}}. (90)

In the implementation, we instead use a stabilized measurement-dependent precision proxy. Zero detected counts are replaced by one count before applying the logarithm. From the resulting post-log measurement yiy_{i}, we first compute

wiraw=1yi+ϵ.w_{i}^{\mathrm{raw}}\;=\;\frac{1}{y_{i}+\epsilon}. (91)

The weights are then normalized, scaled, and clipped:

wi=clip⁡(s​wiraw1m​∑j=1mwjraw+δ,wmin,wmax),w_{i}\;=\;\operatorname{clip}\left(s\,\frac{w_{i}^{\mathrm{raw}}}{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{j}^{\mathrm{raw}}+\delta},w_{\min},w_{\max}\right), (92)

where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 prevents division by small values, δ=10−8\delta=10^{-8} stabilizes the mean normalization, s>0s>0 controls the overall precision scale, and wminw_{\min} and wmaxw_{\max} limit the dynamic range.

We define the fixed effective precision and covariance by

Σ^−1:=diag⁡(w1,…,wm),Σ^:=diag⁡(w1−1,…,wm−1).\widehat{\Sigma}^{-1}\;:=\;\operatorname{diag}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}),\qquad\widehat{\Sigma}\;:=\;\operatorname{diag}(w_{1}^{-1},\ldots,w_{m}^{-1}). (93)

Once computed from the measured sinogram, these matrices are held fixed throughout reconstruction. Unless stated otherwise, subsequent occurrences of Σ\Sigma denote this fixed effective covariance Σ^\widehat{\Sigma}, including the normalization and clipping above.

The resulting weights should be interpreted as a stabilized measurement-dependent precision approximation rather than an unbiased estimator of the ideal Poisson precision.

Validity regime.

The Gaussian approximation is most accurate when all relevant transmitted counts are sufficiently large. At low counts, the normal approximation deteriorates, the logarithmic bias becomes appreciable, and zero-count handling becomes important. A pre-log Poisson model or a hybrid pre-/post-log model can be preferable in that regime [58, 55].

For completeness, the Fisher information of the ideal raw-count model with respect to xx is

ℐ⁡(x)=AΩ⊤​diag⁡(λ1​(x),…,λm​(x))​AΩ.\mathcal{I}(x)\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1}(x),\ldots,\lambda_{m}(x))A_{\Omega}.

Indeed, ∇xλi​(x)=−λi​(x)​ai\nabla_{x}\lambda_{i}(x)=-\lambda_{i}(x)a_{i}, where ai⊤a_{i}^{\top} is row ii of AΩA_{\Omega}, and hence

ℐ⁡(x)=∑i=1m1λi​(x)​∇xλi​(x)​∇xλi​(x)⊤=∑i=1mλi​(x)​ai​ai⊤.\mathcal{I}(x)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}(x)}\nabla_{x}\lambda_{i}(x)\nabla_{x}\lambda_{i}(x)^{\top}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}(x)a_{i}a_{i}^{\top}.

A metric based directly on this quantity would depend on xx. Such a position-dependent metric generally requires additional drift terms in a Riemannian Langevin construction; these terms vanish for the fixed metric used in this work [15].

A.2 Orthogonal Decomposition of the Image Space

This subsection proves the decomposition stated in Section 3.3.

Proof of the orthogonal direct-sum decomposition.

Let r∈ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)r\in\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}) and v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}). There exists z∈ℝmz\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that r=AΩ⊤​zr=A_{\Omega}^{\top}z, and therefore

r⊤​v=z⊤​AΩ​v= 0.r^{\top}v\;=\;z^{\top}A_{\Omega}v\;=\;0.

Thus, ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)⟂𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})\perp\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}). Moreover,

dimℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)+dim𝒩⁡(AΩ)\displaystyle\dim\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})+\dim\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}) =rank⁡(AΩ)+n−rank⁡(AΩ)\displaystyle\;=\;\operatorname{rank}(A_{\Omega})+n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{\Omega})
=n.\displaystyle\;=\;n.

The two orthogonal subspaces therefore span ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, giving

ℝn=ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)⊕𝒩⁡(AΩ),ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)=𝒩​(AΩ)⟂.\mathbb{R}^{n}\;=\;\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})\oplus\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}),\qquad\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})\;=\;\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega})^{\perp}.

∎

A.3 Posterior Geometry Under Incomplete-View CT

Consider

y=AΩ​x+ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ),Σ≻0,y\;=\;A_{\Omega}x+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),\qquad\Sigma\succ 0,

and let p0​(x)p_{0}(x) denote the clean-image prior density. The posterior is

p(x∣y)∝p0(x)exp[−12‖Σ−1/2(AΩx−y)‖22],p(x\mid y)\propto p_{0}(x)\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (94)

which is the standard Bayesian formulation of a linear inverse problem with Gaussian noise [47].

Assume that log⁡p0​(x)\log p_{0}(x) is twice differentiable in a neighborhood of a posterior mode x⋆x^{\star}, and define the local prior curvature by

Hprior​(x⋆):=−∇x2​log⁡p0​(x)|x=x⋆.H_{\mathrm{prior}}(x^{\star})\;:=\;-\left.\nabla_{x}^{2}\log p_{0}(x)\right|_{x=x^{\star}}. (95)

Up to an additive constant, the negative log-posterior is

−log⁡p⁡(x∣y)=−log⁡p0​(x)+12​(AΩ​x−y)⊤​Σ−1​(AΩ​x−y).-\log p(x\mid y)\;=\;-\log p_{0}(x)+\frac{1}{2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}x-y).

Since AΩA_{\Omega} is linear and Σ\Sigma is fixed, taking two derivatives with respect to xx gives

Hpost​(x⋆)=Hprior​(x⋆)+AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ,H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})\;=\;H_{\mathrm{prior}}(x^{\star})+A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}, (96)

where

Hpost​(x⋆):=−∇x2​log⁡p⁡(x∣y)|x=x⋆.H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})\;:=\;-\left.\nabla_{x}^{2}\log p(x\mid y)\right|_{x=x^{\star}}.

Assume that x⋆x^{\star} is a nondegenerate local posterior mode, so that

Hpost​(x⋆)≻0.H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})\succ 0.

To obtain the local Laplace approximation, define the negative log-posterior

ℒ⁡(x):=−log⁡p⁡(x∣y).\mathcal{L}(x)\;:=\;-\log p(x\mid y).

A second-order Taylor expansion around x⋆x^{\star} gives

ℒ⁡(x)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(x) ≈ℒ(x⋆)+∇ℒ(x⋆)⊤(x−x⋆)\displaystyle\;\approx\;\mathcal{L}(x^{\star})+\nabla\mathcal{L}(x^{\star})^{\top}(x-x^{\star})
+12​(x−x⋆)⊤​Hpost​(x⋆)​(x−x⋆).\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}(x-x^{\star})^{\top}H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})(x-x^{\star}).

Because x⋆x^{\star} is a local posterior mode, ∇ℒ​(x⋆)=0\nabla\mathcal{L}(x^{\star})=0. Therefore,

p⁡(x∣y)∝exp⁡[−12​(x−x⋆)⊤​Hpost​(x⋆)​(x−x⋆)]p(x\mid y)\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2}(x-x^{\star})^{\top}H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})(x-x^{\star})\right]

locally around x⋆x^{\star}. This is the kernel of a Gaussian distribution, and hence

p⁡(x∣y)≈𝒩⁡(x⋆,Hpost​(x⋆)−1)p(x\mid y)\;\approx\;\mathcal{N}\!\left(x^{\star},H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})^{-1}\right) (97)

in a neighborhood of the mode [51].

Proposition 3 (Anisotropic posterior curvature).

Suppose Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0. Then:

  1. 1.

    for every v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}),

    AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ​v=0;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}v=0;
  2. 2.

    for every v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}),

    v⊤​Hpost​(x⋆)​v=v⊤​Hprior​(x⋆)​v;v^{\top}H_{\mathrm{post}}(x^{\star})v\;=\;v^{\top}H_{\mathrm{prior}}(x^{\star})v;
  3. 3.

    for every nonzero u∈ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)u\in\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}),

    u⊤​AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ​u>0.u^{\top}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}u>0.
Proof.

If v∈𝒩⁡(AΩ)v\in\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}), then AΩ​v=0A_{\Omega}v=0. The first statement follows immediately, and substitution into (96) proves the second.

For the third statement, let 0≠u∈ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)0\neq u\in\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}). By ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)=𝒩​(AΩ)⟂\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega})^{\perp}, we have u∉𝒩⁡(AΩ)u\notin\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}) and hence AΩ​u≠0A_{\Omega}u\neq 0. Therefore,

u⊤AΩ⊤Σ−1AΩu=‖Σ−1/2AΩu‖22>0.u^{\top}A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}u\;=\;\left\|\Sigma^{-1/2}A_{\Omega}u\right\|_{2}^{2}>0.

This argument does not require AΩA_{\Omega} to have full row rank. ∎

The proposition shows that the likelihood adds no curvature along exact null-space directions and positive curvature along every nonzero direction in ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}). The positive curvature can nevertheless be very small along directions associated with small singular values of Σ−1/2AΩ\Sigma^{-1/2}A_{\Omega}; these are the weakly constrained, or effective null-space, directions discussed in the main text. The resulting posterior covariance also depends on the prior curvature and its cross-directional couplings. It is therefore not generally correct to claim that every null-space direction has larger posterior variance than every range-space direction.

A.4 Projection Operators and Conjugate Gradient Computation

Proposition 4 (Exact orthogonal projectors).

Define

PR:=AΩ⊤​(AΩ​AΩ⊤)†​AΩ,PN:=In−PR,P_{R}\;:=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top})^{\dagger}A_{\Omega},\qquad P_{N}\;:=\;I_{n}-P_{R},

PR2=PR,PN2=PN,PR⊤=PR,PN⊤=PN,PR​PN=PN​PR= 0,PR+PN=In.P_{R}^{2}\;=\;P_{R},\quad P_{N}^{2}\;=\;P_{N},\quad P_{R}^{\top}\;=\;P_{R},\quad P_{N}^{\top}\;=\;P_{N},\quad P_{R}P_{N}\;=\;P_{N}P_{R}\;=\;0,\quad P_{R}+P_{N}\;=\;I_{n}.
Proof.

Let AΩ=Ur​Sr​Vr⊤A_{\Omega}=U_{r}S_{r}V_{r}^{\top} be a compact singular-value decomposition, where SrS_{r} contains the positive singular values. Then

(AΩ​AΩ⊤)†=Ur​Sr−2​Ur⊤,(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top})^{\dagger}\;=\;U_{r}S_{r}^{-2}U_{r}^{\top},

and hence

PR=Vr​Vr⊤.P_{R}\;=\;V_{r}V_{r}^{\top}.

The columns of VrV_{r} form an orthonormal basis of ℛ⁡(AΩ⊤)\mathcal{R}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}), so PRP_{R} is its Euclidean orthogonal projector. The orthogonal complement is 𝒩⁡(AΩ)\mathcal{N}(A_{\Omega}), and therefore PN=In−PRP_{N}=I_{n}-P_{R} is the corresponding null-space projector. All stated identities follow directly. ∎

Regularized range and null filters.

For γ⋆>0\gamma_{\star}>0, define

PR,γ⋆Σ:=AΩ⊤​(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γ⋆​Σ)−1​AΩ.P_{R,\gamma_{\star}}^{\Sigma}\;:=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\star}\Sigma)^{-1}A_{\Omega}. (98)

A.4.1 Matrix-free computation via conjugate gradient

The method uses two types of regularized linear systems. Both coefficient matrices are symmetric positive definite and can be solved by conjugate gradient [22, 21] without forming dense matrices.

Image-space system.

Pullback-metric preconditioning uses

(AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​In)​u=r.(A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n})u\;=\;r. (99)

For p∈ℝnp\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, its matrix–vector product is

(AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​In)​p=AΩ⊤​[Σ−1​(AΩ​p)]+γ​p.(A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n})p\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}[\Sigma^{-1}(A_{\Omega}p)]+\gamma p. (100)

Thus, each CG iteration uses one forward projection, one application of the diagonal precision, and one backprojection.

Measurement-space system.

The approximately null-space-restricted perturbation and the regularized data-consistency correction use

(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γ⋆​Σ)​h=b,γ⋆>0,(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\star}\Sigma)h=b,\qquad\gamma_{\star}>0, (101)

where γ⋆=γnull\gamma_{\star}=\gamma_{\mathrm{null}} for the null-space operation and γ⋆=γproj\gamma_{\star}=\gamma_{\mathrm{proj}} for the data-consistency correction. For p∈ℝmp\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γ⋆​Σ)​p=AΩ​(AΩ⊤​p)+γ⋆​Σ​p.(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\star}\Sigma)p\;=\;A_{\Omega}(A_{\Omega}^{\top}p)+\gamma_{\star}\Sigma p. (102)

For every nonzero pp,

p⊤​(AΩ​AΩ⊤+γ⋆​Σ)​p=‖AΩ⊤​p‖22+γ⋆​p⊤​Σ​p>0,p^{\top}(A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\star}\Sigma)p\;=\;\|A_{\Omega}^{\top}p\|_{2}^{2}+\gamma_{\star}p^{\top}\Sigma p>0,

so the coefficient matrix is symmetric positive definite even when AΩA_{\Omega} is rank deficient.

Remark.

Premultiplying (101) by Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} gives the algebraically equivalent system

(Σ−1​AΩ​AΩ⊤+γ⋆​Im)​h=Σ−1​b.(\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}A_{\Omega}^{\top}+\gamma_{\star}I_{m})h\;=\;\Sigma^{-1}b.

However, its coefficient matrix is generally not symmetric in the Euclidean inner product when Σ\Sigma is non-scalar. Ordinary conjugate gradient should therefore be applied to the symmetric system (101), not directly to this premultiplied form.

Algorithm 2 states the measurement-space recurrence. The same recurrence applies to (99) after replacing the matrix–vector product by (100).

A.5 Pullback Metric and Preconditioned Langevin Dynamics

This subsection concerns the ideal continuous-time process with an exact, time-independent target score. It does not by itself prove that the finite-step practical algorithm, which uses a DDPM score approximation and additional scheduled corrections, produces exact stochastic reconstruction samples.

Let

π(x)∝p0(x)e−Φ⁡(x),Φ(x)=12∥Σ−1/2(AΩx−y)∥22,\pi(x)\propto p_{0}(x)e^{-\Phi(x)},\qquad\Phi(x)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\|\Sigma^{-1/2}(A_{\Omega}x-y)\|_{2}^{2},

and define

Gγ=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​In,γ>0.G_{\gamma}\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n},\qquad\gamma>0.

Because GγG_{\gamma} is constant and positive definite, so is M:=Gγ−1M:=G_{\gamma}^{-1}. Consider

dXs=M∇logπ(Xs)ds+2​MdWs,dX_{s}\;=\;M\nabla\log\pi(X_{s})\,ds+\sqrt{2M}\,dW_{s}, (103)

where WsW_{s} is an nn-dimensional standard Brownian motion and 2​M\sqrt{2M} denotes any matrix LL satisfying L​L⊤=2​MLL^{\top}=2M. The variable ss denotes continuous Langevin time and is distinct from a DDPM timestep.

Since AΩA_{\Omega} and the fixed effective covariance Σ\Sigma do not depend on xx, the metric is independent of position. The metric-derivative terms that arise for a position-dependent Riemannian metric therefore vanish [15].

A.5.1 Fokker–Planck equation and invariance

Let ρ⁡(x,s)\rho(x,s) be the density of XsX_{s}. Under standard regularity and nonexplosion assumptions, its Fokker–Planck equation is

∂ρ∂s=−∇⋅(M∇logπρ)+∇⋅(M∇ρ).\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial s}\;=\;-\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\log\pi\,\rho)+\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\rho). (104)
Lemma 1 (Diffusion covariance for the fixed drift).

Consider the constant-covariance family

dXs=M∇logπ(Xs)ds+LdWs,D:=LL⊤≻0.dX_{s}\;=\;M\nabla\log\pi(X_{s})\,ds+L\,dW_{s},\qquad D\;:=\;LL^{\top}\succ 0. (105)

The density π\pi is invariant for every smooth target in this family if and only if D=2​MD=2M.

Proof.

If D=2​MD=2M, substitution of ρ=π\rho=\pi into the Fokker–Planck equation gives zero because π∇logπ=∇π\pi\nabla\log\pi=\nabla\pi.

Conversely, suppose invariance holds for every smooth target, and set C:=D/2−MC:=D/2-M. Stationarity requires ∇⋅(C∇π)=0\nabla\cdot(C\nabla\pi)=0 for every such π\pi. Choose the standard Gaussian density π(x)∝exp(−∥x∥22/2)\pi(x)\propto\exp(-\|x\|_{2}^{2}/2). Then

∇⋅(C∇π)=(x⊤Cx−trC)π(x).\nabla\cdot(C\nabla\pi)\;=\;(x^{\top}Cx-\operatorname{tr}C)\pi(x).

This expression can vanish for every xx only if C=0C=0, because CC is symmetric. Hence D=2​MD=2M. ∎

Proposition 5 (Invariance and reversibility).

Assume that π\pi is a smooth, strictly positive probability density, ∇log⁡π\nabla\log\pi satisfies conditions ensuring a nonexplosive solution of (103), and the required boundary terms vanish at infinity. Then π\pi is a reversible invariant density of (103).

Proof.

Substituting ρ=π\rho=\pi into (104) gives

∂ρ∂s|ρ=π\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial s}\right|_{\rho=\pi} =−∇⋅(M∇logππ)+∇⋅(M∇π)\displaystyle\;=\;-\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\log\pi\,\pi)+\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\pi)
= 0.\displaystyle\;=\;0.

Thus, π\pi is invariant. Moreover, the stationary probability current is

J(x):=M∇logπ(x)π(x)−M∇π(x)= 0.J(x)\;:=\;M\nabla\log\pi(x)\,\pi(x)-M\nabla\pi(x)\;=\;0.

The vanishing current gives detailed balance and hence reversibility under the stated boundary assumptions. ∎

A.5.2 Discrete-time approximation and matrix-free noise

For an ideal fixed target and a step size ak>0a_{k}>0, Euler–Maruyama gives

X(k+1)=X(k)+akGγ−1∇logπ(X(k))+2​akZ(k),Z(k)∼𝒩(0,Gγ−1).X^{(k+1)}\;=\;X^{(k)}+a_{k}G_{\gamma}^{-1}\nabla\log\pi(X^{(k)})+\sqrt{2a_{k}}\,Z^{(k)},\qquad Z^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\gamma}^{-1}). (106)

The following construction samples Z(k)Z^{(k)} without forming a matrix square root.

Lemma 2 (Matrix-free noise sampler).

Let ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,Im)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}) and c∼𝒩⁡(0,In)c\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) be independent, and define

w=AΩ⊤Σ−1/2ξ+γc,z=Gγ−1w.w\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1/2}\xi+\sqrt{\gamma}\,c,\qquad z\;=\;G_{\gamma}^{-1}w.

Then w∼𝒩⁡(0,Gγ)w\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\gamma}) and z∼𝒩⁡(0,Gγ−1)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\gamma}^{-1}).

Proof.

The vector ww is zero-mean Gaussian and

Cov⁡(w)=AΩ⊤​Σ−1​AΩ+γ​In=Gγ.\operatorname{Cov}(w)\;=\;A_{\Omega}^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}A_{\Omega}+\gamma I_{n}\;=\;G_{\gamma}.

Since Gγ−1G_{\gamma}^{-1} is symmetric,

Cov⁡(z)=Gγ−1​Gγ​Gγ−1=Gγ−1.\operatorname{Cov}(z)\;=\;G_{\gamma}^{-1}G_{\gamma}G_{\gamma}^{-1}\;=\;G_{\gamma}^{-1}.

∎

Drawing ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,In)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}) and using Gγ−1​ξG_{\gamma}^{-1}\xi would instead produce covariance Gγ−2G_{\gamma}^{-2} and is therefore not equivalent.

Euler–Maruyama has weak order one over a fixed finite time interval under standard smoothness and moment assumptions [28]. This fact alone does not prove an O⁡(ak)O(a_{k}) bias for the invariant distribution. Such stationary-bias or nonasymptotic sampling bounds require additional assumptions, such as smoothness and strong log-concavity [10]. Moreover, the practical method uses a time-dependent DDPM score approximation, finite CG solves, scheduled data-consistency corrections, and optional additional perturbations. Proposition 5 therefore justifies the covariance matching in the ideal continuous model; it does not establish exact posterior invariance of the complete finite-step algorithm.

Appendix B Extra Experimental Results

B.1 Single-Image Quantitative Comparison

Table 7 presents a supplementary comparison on a representative test image. For each stochastic diffusion-based method, we generate N=20N=20 reconstructions and compute PSNR and SSIM from their sample mean; FBP produces a single deterministic reconstruction. Because these results are based on only one image, they are intended to illustrate method-specific behavior rather than establish dataset-level performance. The overall observations are broadly consistent with the full 526-image evaluation in Table 2, although the ranking of individual methods may vary between configurations.

In Config i, the proposed method obtains 33.33 dB/0.90, compared with 32.37 dB/0.88 for ReSample. On this image, the corresponding improvements are 0.96 dB in PSNR and 0.02 in SSIM. This result is consistent with the full-dataset trend reported in Table 2.

In Config ii, the proposed method achieves the highest PSNR (28.47 dB), exceeding ReSample by 0.08 dB, and ties with DPS for the highest SSIM at the displayed precision (0.78). In Config iii, it obtains 29.24 dB/0.81, narrowly exceeding ReSample in PSNR (29.21 dB) and achieving a higher SSIM than DPS, PGDM, and ReSample (0.80). DDS performs substantially worse in Configs ii–iv than in Config i. Although this observation is consistent with sensitivity to measurement noise, a single-image comparison cannot determine the underlying cause.

In Config iv, ReSample achieves the highest PSNR (29.55 dB), whereas the proposed method achieves the second-highest PSNR (29.40 dB) and the highest SSIM (0.83). One possible explanation is that a strong data-consistency operation may retain components associated with the ring artifact. Nevertheless, the different PSNR and SSIM rankings only demonstrate a trade-off between reference-based pixel error and structural similarity on this image; they do not by themselves establish the underlying mechanism.

In Config v, the proposed method obtains 33.18 dB/0.90. It exceeds DDS by 1.84 dB in PSNR and 0.02 in SSIM, and ReSample by 4.29 dB and 0.08, respectively. This result is consistent with the intended benefit of adapting the reconstruction update to the directional sensitivity of the limited-angle acquisition geometry. Any causal interpretation should, however, be supported by the geometry ablation and full-dataset evaluation rather than by this single-image comparison alone.

B.2 Sample-Variability Maps for Baseline Methods

Figure 7 compares the pixel-wise sample standard deviation computed from N=20N=20 stochastic reconstructions for each method under the five controlled acquisition settings introduced in Section 4.1.2. The row corresponding to the proposed method is included for direct visual comparison with the diffusion-based baselines. All maps are displayed using the same intensity scale.

As summarized in Table 3, the proposed method has a lower mean pixel-wise sample standard deviation than ReSample in Settings i, iii, iv, and v, whereas ReSample has the lower value in Setting ii. DDS, DPS, and PGDM have higher mean sample variability than the proposed method in all five settings. Spatially, the baseline maps commonly show increased variability around anatomical boundaries and undersampling-related streaks. The proposed method produces comparatively concentrated variability in Settings i, iii, and iv, while its variability increases under noisy or more severely undersampled acquisition, as seen in Settings ii and v.

These results should be interpreted together with reconstruction quality and measurement residuals. High sample variability may indicate measurement-induced ambiguity, but it may also arise from sampling instability. Conversely, low variability may indicate either a concentrated conditional distribution or insufficient exploration by the sampler. Accordingly, the maps should be viewed as empirical sample-variability diagnostics rather than as evidence of calibrated posterior uncertainty. Their spatial patterns are most informative when considered jointly with the posterior-mean and error maps in Figure 2.
